FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in the business of providing networking solutions to its customers. The said activity of the assessee included sale of software packages to customers. For the purpose of its business, the assessee had imported readymade software packages from one ‘H’ of USA. The assessee sold the software packages imported to its customers in the packed condition. The assessee claimed that the payment made by it to ‘H’ for the imports of the software packages was not in the nature of royalty and, therefore, it had no obligation to deduct tax on payment made to ‘H’. The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee’s claim and held that the entire amount paid by the assessee to ‘H’ for the import of the software packages was in the nature of ‘royalty’ and as such was subject to deduction of tax at source as per the provisions of section 195 read with article 12 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and USA, (India-USA DTAA). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the impugned order.

On second appeal :

HELD: Section 9(1)(vi ) provides that royalty receivable by a non-resident from a person in India is deemed to accrue or arise in India. Further, section 90(2) provides that if the provisions of Tax Treaty between India and the country of the non-resident are more beneficial to such non-resident, then the provisions of Tax Treaty shall override the provisions of the Act. [Para 6]

Article 12(3) of the India-USA DTAA defines the term ‘royalty’. As per the India-USA DTAA royalty in respect of the subject-matter of a copyright includes only the payments for the use i.e., exploitation of the copyright of such literary/artistic or scientific work. Therefore, in order to be classified as royalty, the right of the person in possession of the subject-matter of a copyright should be to utilize such copyright in the manner which is otherwise protected by the respective copyright law in favour of the owner of the copyright. The use of the copyright of a copyrighted work is different from use of such work itself. The acquisition of a product, wherein the subject-matter of copyright is embedded, without right to exploit the copyright, does not amount to use or right to use the copyright of such literary/artistic/scientific i.e., copyrighted work. [Para 6.1]

Further, as per clause 13.1 of the OECD model commentary, payments made for acquisition of partial rights in copyright would represent a royalty where the consideration is for the right to use the programmes in a manner that would, without such license, constitute an infringement of the copyright. In other words, the payment can constitute royalty only if the transferor grants to the transferee the right to use the copyright of the product. If, on the other hand, the use of the programmes by the transferee (by acquiring a copy of such programme) is in a manner which does not constitute infringement of the copyright, the payment therefor would not amount to royalty.

CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 42/281 Taxman 19/432 ITR 471 (SC) wherein it was held that amounts paid by resident Indian end-users/distributors to non-resident computer software manufacturers/suppliers, as consideration for resale/use of computer software through EULAs/distribution agreements, is not payment of royalty for use of copyright in computer software - Whether therefore, following aforesaid view Assessing Officer was to be directed to delete impugned addition - Held, yes [Paras 8 and 9] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee, a company incorporated in the USA, was engaged in the business of developing and marketing 3D mechanical design solutions. It entered into software distribution agreements with resellers in India, who buy shrink-wrapped software from the assessee and in turn sell to customers in India.

■

During the relevant assessment year, the assessee received certain sum on account of sale of software solutions which had not been offered for taxation on ground that same were not in nature of royalty.

■

The Assessing Officer treated the receipts as royalty and taxed same at the rate of 15 per cent as per DTAA.

■

The objections raised by the assessee were rejected by the DRP.

■

On appeal :

HELD: ■

The impugned issues are squarely covered in favour of the assessee and against the revenue by the judgment of the High Court of Bombay in assessee’s own case in CIT v. Dassault Systems Solidworks Corporation [IT Appeal No. 302 of 2018, dated 28-06-2023]. [Para 7]

■

This quarrel has attained finality by the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd . v. CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 42/281 Taxman 19/432 ITR 471 (SC). [Para 8]

■

Respectfully following the decision of the High Court and the Supreme Court, the Assessing Officer is directed to delete the impugned addition. [Para 9]

Here, hence is also made to Explanation 2 to section 9(1)(vi) wherein royalty has been defined. As per the definition term royalty envisages payment for transfer of all or any rights in intellectual properties (such as copyrights, patents etc.) by the owner of such intellectual property by any other person. It is clear that the Act does not contain a definition of such intellectual properties that are included within the scope of term royalty. [Para 5.1.2] A retrospective amendment has been made to Explanation to section 9(1)(vi) by Finance Act, 2012. The Finance Act, 2012 inserted Explanation 4 to the section 9(1)(vi) with retrospective effect from 1-6-1976. From the amendment it is clear that it covers the transfer of all or any right for use/right to use of computer software including grant of licence. The amendment has been made to the section i.e., to domestic law. But, there is no corresponding change in Tax Treaty. It is also to be remembered that the assessee had already made the payment before the amendment was introduced. At the point of making payment to ASL, the assessee was not liable to deduct tax at source. So, now it cannot be compelled to deduct tax. The basic principal of taxation stipulates that nobody is supposed to perform the impossible. In the case of B4U International Holdings Ltd. v. Dy. CIT (IT) [2012] 21 taxmann.com 529/52 SOT 545 (Mum.) the Tribunal had held that there is no change in the DTAA between India and USA.

Similar is the position of Indo-UK DTAA, where term royalty has not been defined. Considering same, the definition of term royalty as appearing in the India UK DTAA apply and amendments made by Finance Act, 2012 would have no bearing on the present case. In the instant case, the DTAA is providing particular mode of computation for royalty. As per the agreement the assessee did not have any right to generate the license key or make copies of license key or was provided access to source code in the software. The ASL software products were developed and marketed by it were in the nature of Ashrink-wrap-software-products that are also known as off the shelf software products. The assessee had no role in developing a software, it was just distributing the software to the end users. Therefore, payment by the assessee to ASL for procuring and distributing copyrighted software on principal to principal basis could not be treated as payment towards royalty. ASL was not having a PE in India, therefore, the assessee was not liable to deduct tax at source as per the provision of section 195.[Para 5.1.3]

HEADNOTE: Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with Article 12 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/fees for technical services - Telecom service/transmission services) - Assessment years 2009-10 to 2011-12 - Assessee, a USA based company, was engaged in business of managing, providing and developing billing information and software - Whether, since said payment was neither payment for scientific work nor any patent, trademark, design, plan or secret formula or process said receipt was not Royalty under Article 12 - Held, yes [Para 22] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION: Payment received by assessee, a USA based company, on account of data access/link charges from its Indian subsidiary was neither for scientific work nor any patent, trademark, design, plan or secret formula or process, thus, it could not be held to be 'Royalty' under Article 12 of India-US Tax Treaty  INTERNATIONAL TAXATION: Payment received by assessee for sale of a copyrighted/shrink-wrapped software, which could not be treated as consideration for transfer of any copyright, thus, could not be treated as Royalty under Article 12 of India-US Tax Treaty  INTERNATIONAL TAXATION: Where professional and consultancy services provided by assessee, a USA based company to an Indian company, did not 'make available' any technical knowledge, experience, skill, know-how or process or consist of any development and transfer of any design, receipt on account of said services was not taxable as fee for included services under Article 12 of India-US Tax Treaty

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with Article 12 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/fees for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment years 2009-10 to 2011-12 - Whether for purpose of taxing royalty income covered by Article 12 of India-US Tax Treaty, income should have been generated by 'use of' or 'right to use of' any copyright - Held, yes - Assessee, a USA based company, was engaged in business of managing, providing and developing billing information and software - It received certain amount for sale of off-the shelf/shrink-wrapped software - It also provided certain support and maintenance services in connection with said software - Whether since payment received by assessee was for sale of a copyrighted/shrink-wrapped software, which could not be treated as consideration for transfer of any copyright, thus, could not be treated as Royalty under Article 12 of India-US Tax Treaty - Held, yes - Whether since taxability of aforesaid services was dependent on taxability of software supplied, therefore, receipt from aforesaid services was also not taxable under Article 12(4) - Held, yes [Paras 29 and 32] [In favour of assessee]

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with Article 12 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/fees for technical services - Advisory, consultancy and professional service) - Assessment years 2009-10 to 2011-12 - Assessee, a USA based company, was engaged in business of managing, providing and developing billing information and software - It rendered certain services to an Indian company which comprised of Geneva health check for retail instances and other professional and consultancy services - In return of income, these services were sub-contracted by assessee to Indian Entity on Principle to Principle Basis - Whether since aforesaid services did not 'make available' any technical knowledge, experience, skill, know-how or process or consist of any development and transfer of any design, receipt on account of said services was not taxable as fee for included services under Article 12 of India-US Tax Treaty - Held, yes [Para 41] [In favour of assessee]

headnotes.text: I. Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of India-USA DTAA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment year 2004-05 - Assessee, a tax resident of USA, was engaged in business of developing and marketing of telecommunication equipments and related software - Assessee had entered into agreements with Indian telecommunication companies, such as, Bharti, Tata and Reliance for supply of basic telecom infrastructure equipment software and assisting them to set up telecommunication network - Assessing Officer concluded that receipts from transfer of right to use software was in nature of royalty and since assessee had a branch office in India and agreements with Indian telecommunication companies had been signed in India by an employee of branch office, royalty income was connected to branch office, which constituted permanent establishment (PE) of assessee in India - Thus, he held that receipt would be taxable in India, as royalty income, both under section 9(1)(vi) read with section 115A/44D and article 12 of DTAA - It was noted that hardware and software were supplied together as an integral and inseparable package and hardware and software could not be operated without each other - Agreement between parties made it clear that ownership rights over software remained with licensor - Whether since assessee had not transferred use or right to use, a copyright of a literary, artistic or scientific work so as to fall within definition of royalty under article 12, amount received by assessee from Indian company was not taxable as royalty income - Held, yes - Whether since head office had directly supplied hardware and software from outside territory of India, and neither manufacturing nor any other activities relating to hardware and software supply had taken place in India, in such a scenario, profit/income from offshore supply of equipments and software could not be attributed to PE, as, only such part of income which was relating to operation carried out in India could be attributed to PE and taxed in India - Held, yes [Paras 10-18] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where assessee, US company, had entered into agreements with Indian telecommunication companies for supply of basic telecom infrastructure equipment software and assisting them to set up telecommunication network, since agreement between parties made it clear that ownership rights over software remained with assessee, amount received by assessee from Indian Company was not taxable as royalty income as assessee had not transferred use or right to use, a copyright of a literary, artistic or scientific work so as to fall within definition of royalty under article 12 of India-USA DTAA  INCOME TAX : If contribution towards PF and ESI was paid within grace period provided under PF and ESI Act, same should be allowed as deduction under section 36(1)(va)  INCOME TAX : No interest under section 234B can be charged as assessee, being a non-resident company was not liable to pay advance tax and payer is under an obligation to withhold tax under section 195 while making payment to assessee

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India [Royalties] - Assessment year 2006-07 -Assessee, an American company, purchased PeopleSoft Software which helped in improving visibility, tracking, and control with a single source of information that provided complete, real-time reporting and reconciliation of operational and financial data - Out of total amount incurred by assessee, a proportion of license cost and maintenance cost for PeopleSoft was allocated by assessee to its Indian subsidiary, CIS, which was reimbursed by CIS to assessee - Whether purchase of software would fall within category of copyrighted article and not towards acquisition of any copyright in software and, hence, consideration would not qualify as royalty under article 12 - Held, yes [Para 12.7] [In favour of assessee]

I. Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty and fees for technical services) - Assessment years 2003-04, 2004-05, 2007-08 to 2010-11 - Assessee a US company, earned revenue from licensing of software and supply of "contact solutions" to customers in India which was a combination of software and compatible hardware that enables customers to better manage customer interactions via voice, email, web and fax - Whether consideration received by assessee for supply of 'contact solutions' is not royalty under article 12 of Tax Treaty - Held, yes - Whether since there was no transfer of any right in respect of copyright by assessee and it was a case of mere transfer of a copyrighted article, receipts would constitute business receipts in hands of assessee to be assessed as business income subject to assessee having business connection/ PE in India - Held, yes [Para 42] [In favour of assessee]IT/ILT : Consideration received by assessee for supply of 'contact solutions' used for better management customer interaction, comprising of sale of hardware alongwith license of embedded software to end user is not royalty under article 12 of DTAA between India and USA  IT/ILT : Provision of implementation and maintenance services are inextricably and essentially linked to supply of software; where supply of software is itself not taxable as 'royalty', these services are also not royalty  IT/ILT : Where assessee did not carry on business in India through a building site or construction, there could be no 'installation PE' of assessee in India   IT/ILT : To tax income earned by a US company from customers located outside India under section 9(l)(vi)(c)/9(1)(vii)(c), revenue must prove that customers carry on business in India and that they have used rights in IPs/services for purpose of making or earning income from a source in India

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment year 2016-17 - Assessee, a company incorporated in USA, engaged in development and manufacture of hydraulic and electro-hydraulic and electro-hydraulic controls for off-highway and automotive applications, purchased different software products and transferred some of them to Indian entity at cost, without any markup - Whether since licensors permitted assessee only to install, operate and use their software products to extent of copies purchased by it, without any right to copy same, it could not have transferred anything more than that to its entities globally including India and therefore, there could be no question of treating amount received from Indian entity on transfer of copyrighted articles as royalty in hands of assessee within meaning of article 12(3) - Held, yes [Para 10][In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where assessee, a US based company, purchased different software products and transferred some of them to Indian entity at cost, since assessee itself obtained only a limited access to software products without any right to copy same, it could not have transferred anything more than that to its entities globally including India, therefore, there could be no question of treating amount received from Indian entity on transfer of copyrighted articles as royalty in hands of assessee within meaning of article 12(3) of DTAA between India and USA  INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where assessee, a US based company, purchased certain number of licenses of different software and charged, inter alia, Indian entity for licenses issued, in absence of PE in India, software license fee would not be taxable as business profits

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of the DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India [Royalties/Fees for included services] - Assessee was an international software marketing and development company and its holding company was based in US namely Infrasoft Corporation - Assessee was developing customized software to be used for designing highways, railways, airports, ports, mines, etc. - Software so customized was then licensed to an Indian customer and branch office of assessee in India performed services involving interface to peripheral installation and training etc. - In course of assessment, Assessing Officer taxed receipts on licensing software as 'royalty' as per article 12 of Indo-US DTAA - Tribunal, however, held that amount received by assessee under license agreement for allowing use of software was not royalty either under Act or under DTAA - It was noted that in terms of license agreement, licensee was allowed to make only one copy of software and associated support information for backup purposes with a condition that such copyright would include 'Infrasoft' copyright and all copies of software would be exclusive properties of 'Infrasoft' - It was also apparent that software was to be used only for licensee's own business and without consent of assessee, software could not be loaned, rented, sold, sub-licensed or transferred to any third party - Whether on facts, it was a case of mere transfer of right to use copyrighted material i.e., software programme, and, therefore, amount received by assessee from its Indian customer did not give rise to any royalty income in terms of article 12(3) of India-USA DTAA - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, impugned order passed by Tribunal deleting addition was to be upheld - Held, yes [Para 97] [In favour of assessee]IT/ILT : Amount received by assessee, a non-resident company, for granting license to use its copyrighted software for licencee's own business purpose only, could not be brought to tax as 'royalty' under article 12(3) of India-US DTAA  IT/ILT : In view of fact that assessee-company had PE in India, in terms of decision of Supreme Court in Union of India v. Azadi Bachao Andolan [2003] 263 ITR 706/132 Taxman 373 taxability of income was to be governed by provisions of India-USA DTAA as they were more beneficial to assessee; in absence of any amendment in DTAA, there was no need to examine effect of subsequent amendment to section 9(1)(vi) and also fact as to whether amount received for use of software would be 'royalty' in terms thereof

Section 9, read with section 195, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and article 12 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India [Royalty] - Assessee had entered into a Wireless Software Contract and Wireless Network General Terms and Conditions Contract (GTC) with an Indian company (LTHPL) and another Wireless Software Assignment and Assumption Agreement with LTHPL and an American company for purchase of certain software for purposes of operation of wireless telecommunication network - As per terms of agreements, what was transferred to assessee was only a licence to use copyright belonging to non-resident which continued to be owner of copyright and all other intellectual property rights - Whether payment made by assessee to LTGL and other supplier could be said to be payment for use of or right to use of copyright and it would amount to royalty within meaning of article 12(3) - Held, yes - Whether therefore, assessee was liable to deduct tax at source on such payment - Held, yes [Para 46] [In favour of revenue]IT/ILT-I: Payment for use of copyright belonging to non-resident would amount to royalty within meaning of article 12(3) of DTAA  IT/ILT-II: Where assessee, an American company, had entered into software supply agreement with Indian group company on principal to principal basis and had not deputed any personnel to India, it could not be said to have an agency PE in India as per Indo-US DTAA

Azadi Bachao Andolan [2003] 263 ITR 706/132 Taxman 373, taxability of income was to be governed by provisions of India-USA DTAA as they were more beneficial to assessee; in absence of any amendment in DTAA, there was no need to examine effect of subsequent amendment to section 9(1)(vi) and also fact as to whether amount received for use of software would be 'royalty' in terms thereof - Held, yes [Para 95]

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with articles 12 and 7 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fees for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Assessee, a US company, received a certain consideration for sale of software/license relating to development of software from Indian company - Assessee submitted that amount received from Indian company was not in nature of royalty - Assessing Officer held that receipt was in nature of royalty chargeable to tax in India not only under Act but also under DTAA - Whether since receipt was on account of sale of software/license and not for parting with copyright of software, amount paid for same cannot be brought within ambit of 'royalties' under article 12 of DTAA - Held, yes - Whether further since assessee did not have any PE in India, said sum ceased to be chargeable to tax in India under article 7 - Held, yes [Paras 4 to 6] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Receipt of a certain sum by assessee-US company from Indian company on account of sale of software/license and not for parting with copyright of software was not in nature of 'Royalty'

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty/Fees for technical service - Software) - Assessment year 2014-15 - Assessee courier company, providing specialized courier services and supply chain services, made payment to its US group company - Assessee submitted that there was a Management Information System (MIS) Maintenance Agreement under which said US company, which was proprietor of software, would help group offices located across globe to track movement of courier - Whether where payment was made for sale/license of computer software on a CD/other physical media and end-user only got right to use computer software under a non-exclusive licence ensuring owner continues to retain ownership under section 14(b) of Copyright Act, payments could not be classed as a royalty - Held, yes - Whether issue should be remanded to Assessing Officer to examine terms of Agreement under which right were granted to assessee in light of provisions of DTAA as to whether same would amount to royalty - Held, yes [Para 13] [In favour of assessee/Matter remanded]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where payment was made for sale/license of computer software on a CD/other physical media and end-user only got right to use computer software under a non-exclusive licence ensuring owner continues to retain ownership under section 14(b) of Copyright Act, payments could not be regarded as a royalty
