I. Section  9, read with section 147, of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/fees for technical services - Computer software)- Assessment year 2003-04 - Assessee US company had global and domestic systems software and applications installed on various computing platforms - It entered into an agreement with Indian company, American Express India who catered to needs of various countries and locations - Alleging that assessee had not offered to tax royalty received by assessee from American Express India towards right given for use of Global Makers System, software and application, Assessing Officer sought to initiate reassessment - However, this allegation was factually in correct inasmuch as it was apparent from records that American Express India had filed return of income incapacity of representative assessee for assessee company wherein this royalty income had been offered to tax at rate of 15% per cent under article 12(3)(a) of DTAA - A proper disclosure was made in this regard in return of income filed by assessee in response to notice issued under section 142(1) - Whether it could be said that any new information had come in possession of Assessing Officer so as to warrant invocation of reassessment jurisdiction - Held, no [Para 5.0] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where royalty payment to assessee US company was duly disclosed and offered to tax in return of income filed by Indian company in capacity of representative assessee, reassessment of assessee could not be initiated on ground that assessee had not offered tax on royalty  INTERNATIONAL TAXATION: Where during assessment, assessee US company submitted that it did not have any activity that would constitute PE and furnished agreements with Indian company and assessee's contention was duly accepted by Assessing Officer, re-opening of concluded assessment on ground that assessee had a PE in India was unjustified   INTERNATIONAL TAXATION: Where assessee-US company furnished copies of agreement relating to secondment of employees during assessment which was examined by Assessing Officer and he held that there was no fixed place PE, reassessment on ground that by secondment constituted a fixed place of business of assessee was unjustified

Section  9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty/FTS - Software) - Assessment year 2013-14 - Assessee, a non-resident located in USA, was engaged in business of software development/distribution and rendition of related services - It received consideration from outright sale of software to end user customers in India and claimed same as business income - Assessing Officer treated impugned consideration as royalty payment - Commissioner (Appeals) concluded that consideration received by assessee from outright sale of software was for a copyrighted article and could not be considered as royalty payment - Whether impugned payments were not royalty but were payments made towards purchase of copyrighted article which was to be treated as business income of assessee, not taxable in India in absence of PE of assessee in India - Held, yes - Whether further payments made to assessee were not for any process or for any information concerning industrial, commercial or scientific experience so as to make such payments fall within purview of definition of 'royalty' under India-USA DTAA - Held, yes [Paras 8 and 9] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Amounts paid by resident Indian end users to non-resident computer suppliers as consideration for use of computer software is not payment of royalty

Section 9 ,  read with section 195 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, and article 12 of OECD Model Tax Convention - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty) - Assessment years 2006-07 and 2007-08 - Whether to constitute 'royalty' under India-USA DTAA, it is consideration for transfer of 'use of copyright in work' and not 'use of work' itself; however, 'Explanation 4' inserted under section 9(1)(vi) by the Finance Act, 2012, provides that transfer of rights includes and has always included right to use a computer software including granting of a license - Held, yes - Whether thus, it cannot be said that definition of royalty under Income-tax Act is in pari materia with that under DTAA; Even otherwise, TDS liability does not arise on basis of retrospective amendment in definition of royalty - Held yes - Whether fair use of work for purpose of which it is being purchased and doing of such other acts including making of copy for protection from damage or loss cannot, in any case, be said to be any infringement of copyright, whether or not any license in this respect has been granted by author/owner of work - Held, yes - Assessee-company purchased different types of software from non residents which were used in its business of oil and gas exploration - Software purchased by assessee was a standardized software for use in own business of assessee only - Assessee had not been given any commercial right to reproduce and sell copies of software and party from whom assessee acquired software was not having any permanent establishment (PE) in India and there was no time limit of expiry of said software - Whether consideration paid by assessee as per clauses of DTAA could not be said to be royalty and same would be outside scope of definition of 'royalty' as provided in DTAA and would be taxable as business income of recipient but in absence of P.E. could not be taxed in India - Held, yes [Paras 30  49] [In favour of assessee]

Section 90 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with articles 7 and 12 of the DTAA between India and USA - Double taxation relief - Where agreement exists - Assessment year 2005-06 - Assessee, a US based company, was engaged in manufacturing and selling a software programme - For purposes of marketing its software, assessee entered into agreements with various distributors/resellers in India - Assessee’s case was that software was being sold to customers for their personal use without transfer of any copyright, trademark or patent, etc. - Accordingly, assessee claimed that payment received for supply of software was not royalty but only business income and since it did not have a PE in India, business income so earned was not taxable as per article 7 of Indo-US DTAA - Assessing Officer rejected assessee’s claim taking a view that payment received by assessee for use of software was in nature of royalty as defined under Indo-US DTAA - Accordingly, he brought to tax amount received by assessee - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) set aside order passed by Assessing Officer - Whether in view of order passed by Tribunal in assessee’s own case in respect of earlier assessment year, it was to be held that payment received by assessee was not in nature of royalty within meaning of article 12(3) of Indo-US DTAA and, therefore, impugned order passed by Commissioner (Appeals) was to be upheld - Held, yes

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with Article 12 of the DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Computer software) - In course of appellate proceedings, High Court relying upon order passed in case of CIT (International Taxation) v. ZTE Corpn. [2017] 77 taxmann.com 304/245 Taxman 252/392 ITR 80 (Delhi), held that amount paid by assessee to AE towards embedded software did not constitute royalty - Whether, on facts, SLP filed against order of High Court was to be granted - Held, yes [Para 2] [In favour of revenue]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION: Where High Court relying upon order passed in case of CIT (International Taxation) v. ZTE Corpn. [2017] 77 taxmann.com 304/245 Taxman 252 (Delhi), held that amount paid by assessee to AE towards embedded software did not constitute royalty, SLP filed against order of High Court was to be granted

Section 90 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with articles 7 and 12 of the DTAA between India and USA - Double taxation relief - Where agreement exists - Applicant-Airports Authority of India entered into supply and service contracts with an American company ‘RC’ for Modernisation of Air Traffic Services (MATS) in Delhi and Mumbai - Pursuant to those contracts, ‘RC’ handed over equipment software, etc., and applicant had been operating and maintaining equipments on its own - However, since some assemblies subsequently failed, applicant felt that same needed regular repairs - So, it entered into two separate contracts with ‘RC’ for (a) repair of hardware equipment of MATS system, and (b) modification and anomaly resolution of software of said system - Clauses of supply contract showed that insofar as software and documentation were concerned, applicant acquired a right to use same subject to certain conditions but hardware and other equipment were subject-matter of outright sale in favour of applicant - Whether since payment received by ‘RC’ in respect of repair of hardware, did not fall within meaning of income from rendering of services as defined in article 12, said payment would be regarded as business profits within meaning of article 7 - Held, yes - Whether since ‘RC’ had no Permanent Establishment (PE) in India, said payment would not be taxable in India in view of provisions of article 7 - Held, yes - Whether, accordingly, deputation of an engineer by ‘RC’ to India for purpose of installation and testing of repaired software would not constitute PE of ‘RC’ in India - Held, yes - Whether payment received by ‘RC’ in respect of repair of software fell within description of fees for included services within meaning of article 12 - Held, yes - Whether in view of that description, payment made for repair of software shall be taxable in India - Held, yes

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with articles 5 and 7 of the DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Permanent Establishment - Fixed PE, place of business) - Assessment years 2014-15 and 2015-16 - For relevant years, assessment in case of assessee was completed wherein income from supply of software was treated as royalty by Assessing Officer - It was noted that in earlier years said issue reached to stage of High Court and it was concluded that amount in question was taxable as business profits subject to existence of assessee's PE in India - So far as existence of assessee's PE was concerned, Co-ordinate Bench of Tribunal had remanded said issue back to Assessing Officer for disposal afresh on basis of material on record - Whether in absence of any change in circumstances, following aforesaid orders, impugned order was to be set aside and, matter was to be remanded back to Assessing Officer to decide issue relating to dependent agent/PE in line with direction of Co-ordinate Bench and thereafter decide attribution of income to said PE - Held, yes [Para 17] [Matter remanded]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Following order passed by Co-ordinate Bench in assessee's own case relating to earlier assessment years, matter relating to existence of its dependent agent/PE in India, was to be remanded back for disposal afresh

Section 9 ,  read with section 195 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, and article 12 of OECD Model Tax Convention - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty) - Assessment years 2006-07 and 2007-08 - Whether to constitute 'royalty' under India-USA DTAA, it is consideration for transfer of 'use of copyright in work' and not 'use of work' itself; however, 'Explanation 4' inserted under section 9(1)(vi) by the Finance Act, 2012, provides that transfer of rights includes and has always included right to use a computer software including granting of a license - Held, yes - Whether thus, it cannot be said that definition of royalty under Income-tax Act is in pari materia with that under DTAA; Even otherwise, TDS liability does not arise on basis of retrospective amendment in definition of royalty - Held yes - Whether fair use of work for purpose of which it is being purchased and doing of such other acts including making of copy for protection from damage or loss cannot, in any case, be said to be any infringement of copyright, whether or not any license in this respect has been granted by author/owner of work - Held, yes - Assessee-company purchased different types of software from non residents which were used in its business of oil and gas exploration - Software purchased by assessee was a standardized software for use in own business of assessee only - Assessee had not been given any commercial right to reproduce and sell copies of software and party from whom assessee acquired software was not having any permanent establishment (PE) in India and there was no time limit of expiry of said software - Whether consideration paid by assessee as per clauses of DTAA could not be said to be royalty and same would be outside scope of definition of 'royalty' as provided in DTAA and would be taxable as business income of recipient but in absence of P.E. could not be taxed in India - Held, yes [Paras 30  49] [In favour of assessee]IT/ILT: To constitute 'royalty', it is consideration for transfer of 'use of copyright in the work' and not 'use of work' itself; however, 'Explanation 4' inserted under section 9(1)(vi) by the Finance Act, 2012, provides that the transfer of rights includes and has always included right for use or right to use a computer software including granting of a license and, thus, it cannot be said that definition of royalty under Income-tax Act is in pari materia with that under DTAA

I. Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 5 of DTAA between India and US - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Permanent establishment - Liaison office) - Assessment years 2017-18 to 2020-21 - Assessee, a US based company, was engaged in business of supplying goods from outside India - During relevant period, assessee made offshore sale of goods and offshore sale of software and related support services to its various customers in India - Assessing Officer held that Liaison Office (LO) of assessee in India constituted a PE of assessee in India - Accordingly, he attributed profits to assessee’s PE in India - It was found that assessee had closed its LO operations and no expat employee were engaged by assessee at LO - Revenue had not placed on record any material to show that even after closure of LO operations, assessee still had business connection that could be termed as PE in India - Whether since no business activity was carried out by assessee during relevant period through LO, assessee had no PE in India during impugned assessment year and, hence, question of attribution of profits to PE in India did not arise - Held, yes [Paras 16  20] [In favour of assessee] II. Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment years 2017-18 to 2020-21 - Whether amounts paid by resident Indian end-users/distributions to non-resident computer software manufacturers/suppliers, as consideration for resale/use of computer software through EULAs/distribution agreements, is not payment of royalty for use of copyright in computer software, and thus, same does not give rise to any income taxable in India - Held, yes [Para 23] [In favour of assessee]

Section 9, read with sections 90 and 195, of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and USA and OECD Model Commentary - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India - Assessment years 2000-01 to 2003-04 - Whether as per India-USA DTAA, royalty in respect of subject-matter of a copyright includes only payments for use, i.e., exploitation of copyright of such literary/artistic or scientific work - Held, yes - Whether therefore, in order to be classified as royalty, right of person in possession of subject-matter of a copyright should be to utilize such copyright in manner which is otherwise protected by respective copyright law in favour of owner of copyright - Held, yes - Whether as per clause 13.1 of OECD model commentary, payment can constitute royalty only if transferor grants to transferee right to use copyright of product - Held, yes - Assessee was engaged in business of providing networking solutions to its customers - Said activity of assessee included sale of software packages to customers - For purpose of its business, assessee had imported readymade software packages from one ‘H’ of USA and sold same to its customers in packed condition - Whether payment made by assessee to ‘H’ for import of software packages was in nature of royalty - Held, no - Whether said payment was commercial income which is subject-matter of article 7 of India-USA DTAA but, since ‘H’ did not have permanent establishment in India, assessee had no obligation to deduct tax at source on payment made to ‘H’ - Held, yes

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with articles 7 and 12 of the DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Business profits - Business profit vs. Royalty) - Assessment years 2007-08, 2009-10 to 2012-13 - Assessee was a US based company - It was engaged in sale of licenses of its copyrighted software product called as Project Management Software (PMS) - PMS is considered as a Business Intelligence Tool - It assisted users in regulating and effectively utilizing programmer's time on a collective basis with efficiency - Assessing officer took a view that consideration received by assessee fell in category of 'royalty' - Whether payment received by assessee from its customers from sale of software products/licenses was not in nature of royalty under section 9(1)(vi) of IT Act, 1961 and also as per article 12(3)(a) and article 12(3) (b) of Indo US DTAA - Held, yes - Whether amount received by assessee was normal business income of assessee on account of sale of copy righted products (licenses) and not taxable in India in absence of permanent establishment - Held, yes [Para 34] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Amount received by assessee, a US based company, from sale of copyrighted software products/licences was in nature of business income which in absence of assessee's PE of India, could not be brought to tax said amount was not as 'royalty' under article 12 of India-USA DTAA

Section 9  of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with articles 5 and 12 of the DTAA between India and USA (Permanent establishment) - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India - Assessment year 2007-08 - Assessee, a company incorporated in United States and resident of USA for taxation purposes, was a leading provider of information solutions - In India, it entered into joint venture company with 'NIPL'- In terms of agreement, assessee received certain amount from NIPL towards direct sale of software, which were, subsequently, resold by NIPL to its end customers - Assessee claimed such amount from sale of software as business income and in absence of it having permanent establishment in India as per Article 5 of India-USA treaty, not chargeable to tax - Assessing Officer held that amount declared by assessee as business income from sale proceeds of software represented royalty income covered under article 12(3) - It was noted that as per terms of agreement, product as such had been acquired by NIPL from assessee which was further sold without any modification or alteration - Thus, it was apparent that no license was granted to NIPL for duplicating computer software products of assessee but products as such were sold to NIPL who then resold them to end users on profit - Whether on facts, it was a case of consideration received by assessee for transfer of its copyrighted products and not for transfer of copyrights in computer software programme - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, income arising from sale of copyrighted product was to be considered as business profit and in absence of assessee's PE in India, same could not be brought to tax - Held, yes [In favour of assessee]IT/ILT : Where assessee, a US Company, sold its copyright software programme to joint venture company in India but, there was no transfer of copyright in said software programme, income arising to assessee was to be regarded as business profit and in absence of assessee's PE in India, same could not be brought to tax

I. Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment year 2019-20 - Assessee, a tax resident of USA, had entered into a Software Licensing Agreement for supply of software license in connection with its telecommunication business to its Indian customers and received licence fee - Whether revenue earned from supply of software by assessee on a non-transferable, non-exclusive basis to Indian customers was not taxable as royalty income under provisions of article 12 of India-USA DTAA as same was consideration for sale of a copyrighted software and not for use of any copyright - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Revenue earned from supply of software by assessee, a tax resident of USA, on a non-transferable, non-exclusive basis to Indian customers was not taxable as royalty income under provisions of article 12 of India-USA DTAA as same was consideration for sale of a copyrighted software and not for use of any copyright  INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where receipts from annual maintenance contract was inextricably linked to licence granted by assessee to its licensees and no human intervention was required in provision of AMC services, said receipts were not taxable as FTS in India, same were business profits of assessee not taxable in India in absence of a permanent establishment (PE) of assessee in India

II. Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of the DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/fees for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment years 2010-11 to 2012-13 - Assessee-foreign company entered into a contract with North Delhi Power Limited (NDPL) for offshore supply of software licenses - Whether since no copyright had been transferred to NDPL and only right to use software was given, payment towards software license would not qualify as royalty services even if connected with such software - Held, yes - Whether thus, said payments would also not qualify as FIS under article 12(4) of India US DTAA - Held, yes [Para 37] [In favour of assessee]

I. Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of India-USA DTAA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment year 2004-05 - Assessee, a tax resident of USA, was engaged in business of developing and marketing of telecommunication equipments and related software - Assessee had entered into agreements with Indian telecommunication companies, such as, Bharti, Tata and Reliance for supply of basic telecom infrastructure equipment software and assisting them to set up telecommunication network - Assessing Officer concluded that receipts from transfer of right to use software was in nature of royalty and since assessee had a branch office in India and agreements with Indian telecommunication companies had been signed in India by an employee of branch office, royalty income was connected to branch office, which constituted permanent establishment (PE) of assessee in India - Thus, he held that receipt would be taxable in India, as royalty income, both under section 9(1)(vi) read with section 115A/44D and article 12 of DTAA - It was noted that hardware and software were supplied together as an integral and inseparable package and hardware and software could not be operated without each other - Agreement between parties made it clear that ownership rights over software remained with licensor - Whether since assessee had not transferred use or right to use, a copyright of a literary, artistic or scientific work so as to fall within definition of royalty under article 12, amount received by assessee from Indian company was not taxable as royalty income - Held, yes - Whether since head office had directly supplied hardware and software from outside territory of India, and neither manufacturing nor any other activities relating to hardware and software supply had taken place in India, in such a scenario, profit/income from offshore supply of equipments and software could not be attributed to PE, as, only such part of income which was relating to operation carried out in India could be attributed to PE and taxed in India - Held, yes [Paras 10-18] [In favour of assessee]  II. Section 36(1)(va) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Employees' contribution (General) - Assessment year 2004-05 - Disallowance was made of employees contribution to Provident Fund (PF) and Employees' State Insurance (ESI) paid beyond due date - Assessee submitted that amount in dispute was paid within grace period provided under PF and ESI Act - Whether Assessing Officer was to be directed to verify, whether amount in dispute was remitted to Government account within grace period provided under PF and ESI Act, and if on such verification, Assessing Officer would found assessee's claim to be correct, addition should be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 21-22] [Matter remanded]  III. Section 234B of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Interest - Chargeable as (General) - Assessment year 2004-05 - Whether no interest under section 234B can be charged as assessee, being a non-resident company is not liable to pay advance tax and payer is under an obligation to withhold tax under section 195 while making payment to assessee - Held, yes [Para 25] [In favour of assessee]

Section  9,  read with section 195 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, and article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty) - Assessment years 2008-09 and 2009-10 - Whether where assessee, an Indian company, entered into agreement with US company for use of software owned by US company for internal business operations of assessee and said agreement forbade assessee from decompiling, reverse engineering or disassembling software and also provided that assessee would not sub-license or modify software, consideration payable by assessee was for use of copyrighted article and not for use of copyright and, thus, could not be considered as royalty within meaning of article 12(4) - Held, yes [Para 7][In favour of assessee]IT/ILT: Payment made by assessee to US company for use of software owned by US company, when assessee would use software only for internal business operations and would not sub-license or modify same, could not be considered as royalty within meaning of article 12(4) of DTAA

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Permanent Establishment) - Assessment year 2010-11 - Assessee, a U.S. company, had entered into an agreement with IBM India for supply of software products to IBM India on limited use basis and claimed that sum received by it was not taxable as it was not royalty under article 12 - However, Assessing Officer had held that payments received by assessee were to be characterized as royalty under Act as well as treaty - Assessee had submitted that it had been selling software license without giving right of reproduction and commercial exploitation and it was a typical case of cross border sale which did not lead to taxability in India, and as such in absence of its PE in India, income emanating from software licenses sale was not taxable in India - Tribunal in another case on similar facts held that amount received by assessee was not liable to tax as royalty in India - Whether, on facts, matter should be readjudicated afresh - Held, yes [Para 11] [Matter remanded]IT/ILT : Matter of taxability of payment for licensing of software remanded to file of DRP with a direction to re-decide issue in light of latest decision of Tribunal on same subject

Section 9 ,  read with sections 195 and 90, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and article 12 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and USA (Royalties and fees for included services) - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India - Assessment years 1999-2000 to 2001-02 - Assessee-company was engaged in development of computer software and export of such software - During relevant assessment years it made certain payments for importing software from non-resident companies of USA, France and Sweden - It did not deduct tax at source in respect of such payments on ground that software imported by it was shrink wrap product and same was not customized and no tax was deducted as it was not taxable in India and as payment did not constitute royalty under section 9(1)(vi) and under provisions of DTAA - Whether when licence is granted to make use of software by making copy of same and to store it in hard disk of designated computer and to take back-up copy of software, it is clear that what is transferred is right to use software, an exclusive right, which owner of copyright, i.e., supplier, owns and what is transferred is only right to use copy of software for internal business as per terms and conditions of agreement - Held, yes - Whether when what was transferred in instant case was transfer of copyright including right to make copy of software for internal business, payment made in that regard would constitute royalty for imparting of any information concerning technical, industrial, commercial or scientific knowledge, experience or skill as per clause (iv) of Explanation 2 to section 9(1)(vi) and even as per article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Held, yes - Whether therefore, assessee was liable to deduct tax at source from aforesaid payments - Held, yes [In favour of revenue]IT : When licence is granted to make use of software by making copy of same and store it in hard disk of designated computer and to take back-up copy of software, what is transferred is only right to use copy of software for internal business as per terms and conditions of agreement and payment made in that regard would constitute royalty as per section 9(1)(vi), read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - [India/USA/Article 12 of India-US DTAA/Royalties/Fees for Included services]

I. Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of the India-USA DTAA- Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Others) - Assessment year 2020-21 - Assessee, a tax resident of USA, was engaged in healthcare business for General Electric (GE) group - In year under dispute, assessee received certain amount towards software licence fee cross charged to its affiliates in India which was not offered to tax in India by assessee being reimbursement from affiliates -- Whether since what had been sold to affiliates was copyrighted article and not any right to use copyright, receipts in dispute could not be taxable as royalty income falling under article 12 and alternatively, it could have been taxed as business income under article 7, however, in absence of a Permanent Establishment (PE), it could not be taxed in India - Held, yes [Paras 19 and 20] [In favour of assessee] II. Section 9, read with section 56, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and article 23 of the India-USA DTAA- Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Others) - Assessment year 2020-21 - Whether an item of income, which does not fall under any specific heads of income, such as, salary, house property, business and profession and capital gain, will fall under residuary head 'income from other sources' as per section 56(1) - Held, yes - Whether similarly, article 23(3) of DTAA provides for taxation of residuary items of income which are not dealt with in other articles of DTAA - Held, yes - Whether therefore, where assessee, a tax resident of USA, was engaged in healthcare business for General Electric (GE) group and software licences were sold as tools of business in furtherance of assessee's business activity, receipts therefrom had to be treated as business income and could not be treated as other income under section 56(1) and article 23(3) of DTAA - Held, yes [Paras 18 and 20] [In favour of assessee]

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties or fee for technical services - Software) - Assessment years 2015-16 and 2016-17 - Assessee, an American company, was engaged in business of design, development, manufacture and marketing of digital wireless communication products - It had received an amount from different Indian entities under Brew agreement for grant of license to manufacture various products by using assessee's intellectual property portfolio which included certain software right essential to and/or useful in manufacture and sale of wireless products - Assessing Officer held that income of assessee from licensing of BREW software was taxable under section 9(1)(vi) and under article 12 - Whether since payment in question was made for a software which was for a copyrighted article and not copyright itself, royalty from BREW Operator Agreement was not chargeable to tax in hands of assessee under section 9(1)(vi) as well as article 12 - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where assessee, an American company, was engaged in business of design, development, manufacture and marketing of digital wireless communication products, received an amount from different Indian entities under Brew agreement, since payment was for a software which was for a copyrighted article and not copyright itself, royalty from BREW Operator Agreement was not chargeable to tax in hands of assessee under section 9(1)(vi) as well as article 12 of Indo USA DTAA

Section  9,  read with section  44BB,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and  articles 5  and  12  of the DTAA between India and Canada -  Income deemed to accrue or arise in India (Permanent establishment  - Fixed PE, Place of Business) - Assessment year  2022-23  - Assessee, a Canadian company engaged in sale of reservoir simulation software used in oil and gas exploration industry and in providing software maintenance/support services, granted software licences to Indian customers - It claimed that receipts from software licences and maintenance services were exempt in India under India-Canada DTAA - Assessing Officer treated software licence receipts as royalty and software maintenance fees as fee for included services, while DRP held in addition that assessee had a PE in India and entire receipts were taxable under section 44BB - It was noted that in preceding assessment years Tribunal had held that assessee had no PE in India and identical receipts were not taxable in India - Whether since revenue failed to establish existence of PE in India, impugned order taxing receipts under article 12 or section 44BB was liable to be set aside - Held, yes [Paras 10 and 12] [In favour of assessee]

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/fees for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee, a USA based company, was engaged in business of development of mathematical computing software for engineers and scientists - It sold software licence to its distributor in India who in turn sold same to end-users - Assessing Officer held that amount received by assessee was royalty within meaning of article 12 of India-US Tax Treaty and also as per provisions of section 9(1)(vi) - It was noted that Commissioner (Appeals) had categorically held that assessee had only permitted end-users to use a copyrighted article and there was no sale of copyright per se in said article - Whether in light of categoric finding by Commissioner (Appeals) that end-users were only granted a non-exclusive / non-transferrable and a non-sub-licensable licence, payment received by assessee from Indian company on sale of software to end-users could not be termed as "royalty" under relevant DTAA - Held, yes [Paras 6 and 7] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where assessee, a US based company, received consideration for sale of software licences to its distributor in India who in turn sold same to end-users, since assessee only permitted end-users to use a copyrighted article and there was no sale of copyright per se in said article, payment received by assessee from said distributor on sale of software to end-users could not be termed as 'royalty' under relevant DTAA  INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where assessee, a US based company, received consideration towards maintenance services in relation to sale of software licences in India, since said maintenance services were inextricably linked to supply of software licence and when supply of software itself was not taxable as 'royalty', amount received by assessee on account of said maintenance services could not be termed as 'fees for included services'

I. Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment year 2019-20 - Assessee, a tax resident of USA, had entered into a Software Licensing Agreement for supply of software license in connection with its telecommunication business to its Indian customers and received licence fee - Whether revenue earned from supply of software by assessee on a non-transferable, non-exclusive basis to Indian customers was not taxable as royalty income under provisions of article 12 of India-USA DTAA as same was consideration for sale of a copyrighted software and not for use of any copyright - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]II. Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with articles 7 and 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Make available) - Assessment year 2019-20 - Assessee, a tax resident of USA, had provided software license in connection with its telecommunication business to Reliance - It had also provided support and maintenance services in from of Annual Maintenance Contract (AMC) services - Assessing Officer treated AMC charges as Fee for Technical Services (FTS) - It was observed that Assessing Officer had himself acknowledged fact that support and maintenance services were inextricably linked to licence granted by assessee to its licensees and no separate contract was entered by assessee for same - Further, said activities did not make available any technical knowledge to employees of Reliance and/or human intervention was required in provision of AMC services - Whether, in view of above, impugned receipts were not taxable in India as FTS/FIS under article 12(4) of India-USA DTAA but was business profits of assessee not taxable in India in absence of a Permanent Establishment (PE) of assessee in India - Held, yes [Paras 10 and 11] [In favour of assessee]

Section 9, read with section 195, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and Article 12 of the DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to Accrue or Arise in India - Royalties - Assessment year 2007-08 - Assessee-company was in business of providing IT enabled services in investment banking, securities trading and other financial services - Assessee engaged 'I', USA to provide software services in relation to certain accounting systems of assessee for which it made payments without deducting tax at source - Assessing Officer was of view that payments made for services rendered by 'I' USA amounted to fees for technical services as it fulfilled conditions contemplated in article 12(4) of India-USA DTAA and was therefore, taxable in India - On appeal, it was noted that in assessment proceedings issue was confined to holding as to whether payment was taxable in India under article 12 of India-USA DTAA - However, there was no determination as to whether or not payment made to consultant 'I', USA, for services rendered was in nature of royalty as contemplated by provisions of section 9(1)(vii) thereby attracting provisions of TDS - Whether in view of above, impugned order was to be set aside and, matter was to be remanded back for disposal afresh - Held, yes [Para 5.3] [Matter remanded]IT/ILT : Where there was no determination as to whether payment made by assessee to a US based company for rendering software services in relation to its accounting system amounted to royalty under section 9(1)(vii) and, thereby attracting provisions of TDS, matter was to be remanded back for disposal afresh

Section 9, read with section 195, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and article 12 of the DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty/Fees for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment years 2010-11 to 2017-18 - Assessee, a US-based company, earned revenue from software sales to Indian clients - Assessing Officer deemed this revenue as royalty under article 12, subjecting it to Indian taxation - However, Tribunal, ruled in favour of assessee, stating that revenue from software sales should not be taxed as royalty - Even according to revenue issue was covered against it by judgment rendered by Supreme Court in Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 42/281 Taxman 19/432 ITR 471 (SC) wherein Apex Court held that payment made to non-resident computer software suppliers for resale/use of computer software through End User Licensing Agreement (EULAs)/distribution agreements, was not payment of royalty for use of copyright in computer software under various relevant tax treaties and accordingly, in terms of section 195, payer was not required to withhold tax at source at time of making payments to non-resident supplier - Revenue however, informed that a review petition had been filed qua aforesaid judgment - In those circumstances, High Court closed above-captioned appeals but held that in case, review petition was decided against assessee, then assessee would be at liberty to approach Court to reopen appeals - Revenue filed instant SLP after a delay of 384 days - Whether since explanation offered for delay was not satisfactory, SLP filed against impugned order of High Court was to be dimissed - Held, yes [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : SLP dismissed against order of High Court that where assessee, a US based company earned revenue from software sales to Indian clients, said revenue could not be treated as royalty and subjected to Indian taxation

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with articles 5 and 7 of the India-Finland DTAA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Permanent establishment - Agency PE) - Assessment years 2008-09, 2009-10, 2010-11, 2013-14, 2014-15 and 2015-16 - Whether assessee company's worldwide net profit margins as per its audited accounts were to be applied for determining quantum of income to be attributed to PE - Held, yes - Whether thus payments made by assessee to its Indian AE were to be allowed as deduction from gross profits figure and if after such deduction there was loss, in such case no profit or income would be attributable to PE - Held, yes [Paras 28 and 29] [In favour of assessee]  Section 9 of the Income-Tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of the India-Finland DTAA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment years 2008-09, 2009-10, 2010-11, 2013-14, 2014-15 and 2015-16 - Assessee, a Finland based company, supplied software along with supply of telecom equipments to Indian companies - For customs duty purpose value of software was shown separately in invoice - Assessing Officer held that amount charged for software was to be charged as royalty under article 12 and would be taxable in India - In case of DIT v. Ericsson AB [2011] 16 taxmann.com 371/[2012] 204 Taxman 192 which was factually similar to assessee’s case it was held by High Court that payment received by assessee was towards title and hardware of which software was an inseparable part incapable of independent use and it was a contract for supply of goods and, therefore, no part of payment could be classified as payment towards royalty - Whether following aforesaid view, software sales could not give rise to royalty income taxable in India - Held, yes [Para 40] [In favour of assessee]

II. Section  9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of the India-USA DTAA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/fees for technical services - Engineering services) - Assessment year 2015-16 - Assessee US based company purchased software from third-party vendor outside India for and on behalf of its AE in India and made payment of software charges for same - Assessee claimed software charges recovered from its AE as reimbursement on an 'at-cost' basis and without any profit element and, accordingly, did not offer it for tax - Assessing Officer treated reimbursement of software charges received by assessee as royalty under section 9(1)(vi) and article 12 of DTAA - It was noted that assessee did not render any service in connection with such reimbursement of software charges by AE - Whether once character of payment received by assessee was found to be in nature of reimbursement of expenses, it could not be considered as income chargeable to tax as royalty - Held, yes [Para 32] [In favour of assessee]

II. Section  9  of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA -  Income deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties or Fees For Technical Services  - Computer Software) - Assessment years  2001-02 to 2004-05  -Assessee-company, incorporated in USA, had a wholly owned subsidiary in India, namely, OIPL, which carried on software distribution and software development support activities - In respect of global software licensing deals entered into outside India, revenue attributable to India was transferred to OIPL under Software Support Services Agreement - Assessing Officer held that such revenue transfers on global deals represented royalty under section 9(1)(vi) read with article 12(7)(b) and brought same to tax in hands of assessee - It was noted that under said agreement, OIPL was only granted licence to use software and render support services and did not undertake any duplication of software in India, and there was no contractual obligation on OIPL to pay royalty to assessee on revenue transfers - Whether revenue transfers on global deals were not chargeable to tax in India as royalty under section 9(1)(vi) or article 12 of DTAA - Held, yes [Paras 44 to 48] [In favour of assessee]

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/fees for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee, a USA based company, was engaged in business of development of mathematical computing software for engineers and scientists - It sold software licence to its distributor in India who in turn sold same to end-users - Assessing Officer held that amount received by assessee was royalty within meaning of article 12 of India-US Tax Treaty and also as per provisions of section 9(1)(vi) - It was noted that Commissioner (Appeals) had categorically held that assessee had only permitted end-users to use a copyrighted article and there was no sale of copyright per se in said article - Whether in light of categoric finding by Commissioner (Appeals) that end-users were only granted a non-exclusive / non-transferrable and a non-sub-licensable licence, payment received by assessee from Indian company on sale of software to end-users could not be termed as "royalty" under relevant DTAA - Held, yes [Paras 6 and 7] [In favour of assessee]Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/fees for technical services - Information technology support services) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Whether in view of facts and circumstances under heading "Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/fees for technical services - Computer software)", where assessee company recieved amount towards maintenance of software sold by it to its distributor in India who in turn sold same to end users, since said receipt was on account of maintenance which was inextricably linked to supply of software licence and when supply of software itself was not taxable as 'royalty', impugned receipt could not be termed as 'fees for included services', and accordingly, same could not be taxed under provisions of article 12(4)(a) of India-US DTAA - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of the DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Computer Software) - Assessee-company paid licence fee to AE for using software owned by it - High Court took a view that licence fee was not 'royalty' because copyright in software was not transferred, but same was merely allowed to be used - Whether, on facts, SLP filed against order of High Court was to be granted - Held, yes [Para 3] [In favour of revenue]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION: Where High Court took a view that license fee paid by assessee to its AE for using software owned by it did not constitute royalty because copyright in software was not transferred, but same was merely allowed to be used, SLP filed against order of High Court was to be granted

Section  9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty or fees for technical software) - Assessment year 2001-02 and 2002-03 - Assessee-company was engaged in business of development of software - During relevant years assessee made payment of licence fee to a US based company for using software owned by said company - Assessing Officer took a view that licence fee so paid was taxable in India as royalty - Tribunal upheld order of Assessing Officer - Whether payments made by assessee company to US company for user of its software, logo and trademarks were in nature of royalty covered under article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, impugned order passed by Tribunal was to be upheld - Held, yes [Para 8] [In favour of revenue]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION/TRANSFER PRICING: Where assessee-company made payment of licence fee to a US based company for using software owned by said company, such payment was royalty covered under article 12 of DTAA between India and USA

Section 9, read with section 90, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties or Fees For Technical Services - Computer Software) - Assessment year 2022-23 - Assessee, a tax resident of USA, received consideration of Rs. 4.69 crores from licensing of software to RJIL and Rs. 27.84 lakhs from support and maintenance services - Assessee claimed that these were business income not chargeable to tax in India in absence of any PE - Assessing Officer held that right imparted was to use a proprietary process taxable as process/copyright royalty, and that support and maintenance were inextricably linked to license and constituted FTS with 'make available' test satisfied - Accordingly, Assessing Officer proposed to assess entire receipts as FTS taxable at 10 per cent under Article 12 of DTAA - It was noted that in assessee's own case for earlier assessment year, Tribunal held that consideration for both software licensing and support services (AMC) was not taxable in India as 'Royalty' or 'Fees for Technical/Included Services' under Article 12 of India–USA DTAA, but constituted non-taxable business income in absence of a Permanent Establishment - Whether since payment received by assessee during year had been received by virtue of same agreement which was effective in earlier assessment year and nature of payment also remained same, following aforesaid order of Tribunal, addition made by Assessing Officer as income from FTS/FIS was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 6.1] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION: Where assessee, a USA tax resident, received consideration from licensing of software and support services to RJIL under same agreement and circumstances as prior year, and Tribunal had previously held such receipts to be non-taxable business income in absence of any Permanent Establishment, addition made by Assessing Officer as FTS/FIS was to be deleted

Section 9 , of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of the DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties and fees for included services) - Assessment year 2006-07 - Assessee made payment towards purchase of software to US based company - Assessee claimed that 'Off Shelf software' purchased by it did not have tax implication in India inasmuch as assessee had not purchased any copyright in software but only a copyright product - Assessing Officer held that amount paid to US based company for purchase of software was taxable in hands of said company under section 9(1)(vi) as also under applicable tax treaty - Held that while payment for use of copyright is indeed covered by definition of 'royalty', payment for use of copyright article would not be covered by definition of 'royalty' - Accordingly, amount received by US based company was held to be not taxable in India as 'royalty' [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]

Section 9, read with section 90, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties or Fees For Technical Services - Computer Software) - Assessment year 2022-23 - Assessee, a tax resident of USA, received consideration of Rs. 4.69 crores from licensing of software to RJIL and Rs. 27.84 lakhs from support and maintenance services - Assessee claimed that these were business income not chargeable to tax in India in absence of any PE - Assessing Officer held that right imparted was to use a proprietary process taxable as process/copyright royalty, and that support and maintenance were inextricably linked to license and constituted FTS with 'make available' test satisfied - Accordingly, Assessing Officer proposed to assess entire receipts as FTS taxable at 10 per cent under Article 12 of DTAA - It was noted that in assessee's own case for earlier assessment year, Tribunal held that consideration for both software licensing and support services (AMC) was not taxable in India as 'Royalty' or 'Fees for Technical/Included Services' under Article 12 of India–USA DTAA, but constituted non-taxable business income in absence of a Permanent Establishment - Whether since payment received by assessee during year had been received by virtue of same agreement which was effective in earlier assessment year and nature of payment also remained same, following aforesaid order of Tribunal, addition made by Assessing Officer as income from FTS/FIS was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 6.1] [In favour of assessee]

Section 9, read with section 195, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties or fees for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment years 2011-12 and 2012-13 - Whether amount paid by assessee Indian end-users/distributors to non-resident computer software manufacturer/suppliers as consideration for resale/use of computer software through EULAs/distribution agreement was not payment of royalty for use of copyright in computer software and, thus, said payment did not give rise to any income taxable in India - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Amount paid by assessee Indian end-users/distributors to non-resident computer software manufacturer/suppliers as consideration for resale/use of computer software through EULAs/distribution agreement was not payment of royalty for use of copyright in computer software and, thus, said payment did not give rise to any income taxable in India

Section 9 ,  read with section 40(a)(i), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and article 12 of the DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalty) - Assessment year 2011-12 - Assessee sold software to 'ESI India' and in assessment of 'ESI India' payments were treated as towards purchase of software and not as payment towards Royalty - Whether when payment in question was not treated as royalty in hands of purchaser, then same status should also be extended to other party of same transaction and, thus, in present case, income towards sale of software to Indian AE could not be treated as 'Royalty' in hands of US-AE - Held, yes [Para 8] [In favour of assessee]IT/ILT: Where a payment was treated as sale consideration in hands of purchaser Indian AE, same could not be treated as royalty in hands of seller US-AE

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fee for technical services - Computer software) - Assessment years 2005-06 and 2007-08 - High Court by impugned order held that payments made by Indian-company to assessee, a non-resident company, for resale/use of computer software through distribution agreements, did not amount to royalty for use of copyright in computer software and same did not give rise to any income taxable in India - Whether notice was to be issued in SLP filed by revenue against impugned order of High Court - Held, yes [Para 1] [In favour of revenue]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Notice issued in SLP filed against impugned order of High Court that where payments were made by an Indian company to American company for resale/use of computer software through/distribution agreements, said payment did not amount to royalty for use of copyright in computer software

Section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 12 of the DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Royalties/Fees for included services) - Assessment year 2008-09 - Assessee, a US company, entered into agreements with various customers in India for rendering software services - Assessing Officer held that payments received by assessee from sale of software and provision of maintenance and other support services to customers in India, were taxable as 'royalty' and accordingly made additions - Whether in view of decision of Jurisdictional High Court in case of DIT v. Infrasoft Ltd. [2014] 220 Taxman 273/[2013] 39 taxmann.com 88 (Delhi), payment received by assessee from sale of software and provisions of maintenance and other supports services to customers in India were not taxable as 'royalty', in terms of section 9(1)(vi) as well as article 12 of India US Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement - Held, yes - Whether thus therefore impugned additions were to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]IT/ILT: In view of decision of Jurisdictional High Court in case of DIT v. Infrasoft Ltd. [2014] 220 Taxman 273/[2013] 39 taxmann.com 88 (Delhi), addition made for sale of software and provisions of maintenance/other support services to customers in India being not taxable was to be deleted

facts.text:
The assessee, a tax resident of USA, was engaged in the business of developing and marketing of telecommunication equipments and related software. The assessee had entered into agreements with certain India telecommunication companies, such as, Bharti, Tata and Reliance for supply of basic telecom infrastructure equipment software and assisting them to set up telecommunication network. The assessee had a branch office in India.

The Assessing Officer noticed that though the assessee had receipts from certain Indian companies, however, the assessee had not offered such receipts to tax.

The assessee submitted that it had sold the software along with hardware (equipments) on outright sale. The assessee submitted that the software sold by the assessee was embedded in the hardware and only for the purpose of operating hardware. Therefore, it could be treated as royalty.

Referring to agreements entered with various Indian telecommunication companies, such as, Bharti, Tata, and Reliance, the Assessing Officer concluded that the receipts from transfer of right to use the software were in the nature of royalty and the assessee had a branch office in India and as the agreements with the Indian telecommunication companies had been signed in India by an employee of the branch office, the royalty income was connected to the branch office, which constituted permanent establishment (PE) of the assessee in India. Thus, he held that the receipts would be taxable in India, as royalty income, both under section 9(1)(vi), read with section 115A/44D as well as under the India-USA DTAA, since, the assessee had a PE in India in terms of article 5. He further observed, even assuming assessee's claim that the receipts were not in the nature of royalty income was correct, still they would be taxable as business profits under article 7(1) of the treaty, as, the assessee had a PE in India.

The Commissioner (Appeals) held that insofar as receipts from Bharti and Tata were concerned, since the assessee had transferred limited, non-transferable, non-exclusive right to use the software solely in the operation of telecommunication equipments purchased by them, such receipts could not be treated as royalty income. However, he observed, since, the agreement with Reliance was, differently worded, in the sense, that a perpetual, irrevocable, exclusive, unrestricted licence had been granted, the receipts from Reliance would be taxable as royalty income and receipts from supply of software as business profit were taxable as business profit under article 7 of India-USA DTAA as the assessee had a PE in India and such receipts were integrally connected to the PE.

The assessee, a company incorporated in the United States and resident of USA for taxation purposes, was a leading provider of information solutions. The company operated globally through the presence of subsidiaries in other countries. In India, it entered into joint venture company with 'NIPL' which acted as a distributor for the company and imported certain software from the assessee and duplicated and sold or sometimes resold the same in the Indian sub-continent. It was noticed by the Assessing Officer that in the relevant assessment year, the assessee received royalty as per the distribution agreement amounting to Rs. 1.76 crore towards sales made by NIPL which was offered by the assessee as royalty income. The Assessing Officer accepted the said amount as royalty income and taxed it accordingly. The assessee was also found to have received a sum of Rs. 58.29 lakhs from NIPL towards the direct sale of software, which were subsequently resold by NIPL to its end customers. The assessee claimed such amount from sale of software as business income and in the absence of it having permanent establishment in India as per article 5 of India-USA treaty, not chargeable to tax.

The A.O. held that a sum of Rs. 58.29 lakh declared by the assessee as business income from the sale proceeds of software also represented royalty income covered under article 12(3) of the DTAA. In his opinion there was no difference between two situations viz., firstly, in which the NIPL acquired the right to duplicate for which the assessee received income of Rs. 1.76 crore and; secondly in which NIPL acquired software as such from the assessee for a sale consideration of Rs. 58.29 lakh. He, therefore, treated the entire amount of Rs. 2.34 crore as royalty income and charged tax accordingly. The Commissioner (Appeals) echoed the assessment order.

On second appeal:

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of providing networking solutions to its customers. The said activity of the assessee included sale of software packages to customers. For the purpose of its business, the assessee had imported readymade software packages from one ‘H’ of USA. The assessee sold the software packages imported to its customers in the packed condition. The assessee claimed that the payment made by it to ‘H’ for the imports of the software packages was not in the nature of royalty and, therefore, it had no obligation to deduct tax on payment made to ‘H’. The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee’s claim and held that the entire amount paid by the assessee to ‘H’ for the import of the software packages was in the nature of ‘royalty’ and as such was subject to deduction of tax at source as per the provisions of section 195 read with article 12 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and USA, (India-USA DTAA). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the impugned order.

On second appeal :

■

The assessee, a US company and tax resident of the USA under the India–USA DTAA, filed its return for assessment year 2001-02. It had a wholly owned Indian subsidiary, OIPL, with two divisions: (i) Software Distribution, duplicating and distributing software in India under a Software Duplication and Distribution License Agreement (SDDLA) with the assessee, paying royalty on such duplication; and (ii) Software Development Support, performing support functions (translation, porting, customisation, localisation) outsourced by the assessee under a separate agreement.

■

The Assessing Officer first held in assessment year 2001-02, and continued for subsequent years, that OIPL constituted the assessee’s PE in India in respect of software development activities, alleging: (a) a Fixed Place PE on the basis that premises in India and machinery/equipment there were of/at the disposal of the assessee; (b) a Service PE relying on hiring/employee presence in India as inferred from the assessee’s group Form 10-K; and (c) an Agency PE on the footing that OIPL acted for the assessee. The Assessing Officer attributed about Rs. 4.96 crores as profits to the alleged Indian PE for R&D activities.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals), by consolidated orders (covering assessment years 1997-98 to 2004-05 and separately assessment year 2005-06), confirmed the Assessing Office’s finding that OIPL constituted the assessee’s PE in India and sustained attribution of profits.

■

On the assessee’s appeals to the Tribunal:

The assessee was a company incorporated in USA. It entered into an agreement with a software company, Oracle, in terms of which it obtained non-exclusive user right of a software owned by said company.

The assessee had two subsidiaries in India namely, CIL and CDS. It agreed to grant those companies user rights of software acquired from Oracle.

The assessee claimed that fees received from CIL and CDS for granting right to use software in question could not be treated as royalty or fee for technical services.

The assessee thus treated said income as business profit under Article 7 of the DTAA between India and USA and since it did not have PE in India income in question was claimed as exempt.

The Assessing Officer, however, opined that the payments received were royalty covered under section 9(1)(vi) and same was taxable in the hands of the assessee in India.

The Assessing Officer also examined the Articles of DTAA between India and USA and held that the amount of fee partook the character of the royalty within the meaning of Article 12(3) of the DTAA and, thus, it was taxable in the source country i.e. India.

The DRP confirmed the order passed by Assessing Officer.

On appeal:

The assessee-company was incorporated under the laws of USA. It was provider of products and services for automating the management, compliance and secure use of open source software in multi source development at enterprise scale. During the year under consideration, the assessee had sold software under a 'Master License and Subscription Agreement' with two entities in India, namely, (a) Infosys Limited; and (b) Robert Bosch Engineering.

In course of assessment, the Assessing Officer concluded that receipts of assessee pertaining to licensing of software were taxable as royalty under section 9(1)(vi). Thereafter, he proceeded to hold that even under the treaty, the payment received by the assessee was in the nature of royalty within the terms of article 12(3) of India-USA DTAA.

The DRP upheld the order of Assessing Officer.

On appeal:

The assessee was an international software marketing, and development company and its holding company was based in US namely Infrasoft Corporation.

The assessee was developing customized software to be used for designing highways, railways, airports, ports, mines, etc. The software so customized was licensed to an Indian customer and the branch office of the assessee in India performed services involving interface to peripheral installation and training etc.

In course of assessment, the Assessing Officer taxed the receipts on licensing the software as 'royalty' as per article 12 of Indo-US DTAA.

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of Assessing Officer.

The Tribunal, however, held that the amount received by the assessee under the license agreement for allowing the use of the software was not royalty either under the Act or under the DTAA.

On revenue' appeal:

The applicant, an Indian company, entered into an agreement with a non-resident American company for securing license of a particular software, which the applicant is entitled to use. The applicant has to pay license fee for the same to the American company. According to the applicant, the said company does not have any establishment/office in India and, therefore, the payments received by it from the applicant, for allowing it to download and use the software, are covered under article 7 of the DTAA, i.e., business profits, which are not chargeable to tax in India. On these facts, the applicant sought ruling of the Authority as regards the question as to whether periodical payments made by it to the American company in connection with the use of software developed by it on internet are subject to tax deduction at source under DTAA with USA. The jurisdictional Commissioner submitted his comments stating, inter alia, that as per Explanation 2 to section 9(1)(vi), the use of software falls under the category of 'royalty' and, consequently, payments would be covered under article 12 of the DTAA and the applicant is liable to deduct tax at source while making payment to that non-resident person.

The assessee was a marketing and development company of an international group, owned by its holding company incorporated outside India. The said group was a leader in civil engineering software and had developed a software called Mx, which was used for civil engineering works in various countries throughout the world. Based on the market position and business potential of the said software and related products in India, a branch office of the group was established in India after obtaining necessary approval, mainly for import and supply of software and also to provide support services including system related services such as, installation of software; interface to peripherals; uninstallation; imparting of training on the application of software, etc. For the relevant assessment year, the assessee filed the return of income showing the receipts from sale/licensing of the software. It claimed that it was entitled to deduction of purchase cost of software, as well as other related expenses from the aforesaid receipts and the net profit so arrived at alone could be taxed as its business profit as per Article 7 of the DTAA. The Assessing Officer rejected its claim holding that the entire amount received by the assessee-company from transfer of software as well as other incidental services, such as installation of software; imparting of training, etc., was in the nature of royalty under section 9(1)(vi) and such royalty income having been accrued or arisen to the assessee-company through its PE in the form of its branch office in India, the same was chargeable to tax in India as per Article 13(6) of the DTAA. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

■

The assessee, a company incorporated in Canada and a tax resident of Canada, was engaged in selling reservoir simulation software used in oil and gas exploration industry and in providing software maintenance / support services. In India, it granted software licences to customers in oil and gas sector and to an educational institution. For assessment year 2022-23, it claimed that receipts from sale of software licences and software maintenance/support services were exempt in India under India–Canada DTAA. Similar additions on these streams had arisen in earlier years, and Assessing Officer noted that there was no difference in nature of receipts vis-à-vis preceding years.

■

In draft assessment order, Assessing Officer treated receipts from sale of software licences of Rs. 3.04 crores as royalty under article 12 and proposed to tax software maintenance fees of Rs. 9.62 crores as fee for included services under article 12(4), recording that facts were similar to those in earlier assessment years beginning from assessment year 2012-13.

■

On objections, DRP recharacterized software licence receipts as ‘equipment royalty’ under article 12(3)(b), upheld proposal to tax software maintenance fees as fee for included services under article 12(4), and further concluded that assessee had a PE in India, holding in alternative that entire receipts were taxable under section 44BB. DRP acknowledged that facts were identical to assessment years 2020-21 and 2021-22.

■
