III. Royalty Contrary to the expectation that the retrospective amendment in respect of royalty will provide some finality, litigation on the issue has continued unabated. There is a sense of "déjà vu" inasmuch as different High Courts have once again taken differing views on taxability of income as 'royalty.'

In September 2012, in the case of DIT v. Nokia Networks OY [2013] 212 Taxman 68/[2012] 25 taxmann.com 225 the Delhi High Court held that payment for supply of software imbedded in hardware was not taxable as royalty under Article 13 of the India-Finland DTAA. Relying on its own ruling in DIT v. Ericsson A.B. [2012] 343 ITR 470/204 Taxman 192/16 taxmann.com 371, Delhi High Court rejected the arguments of the Revenue that the question of copyright and copyrighted article was not relevant for the taxability of software under the Act or the DTAA and that the 'right to use' simpliciter of software was a part of the copyright in the software, irrespective of whether a further right to make copies is granted. Delhi High Court observed that the language of the India-Finland DTAA differed from amended section 9(1)(vi) and retrospective amendment could not be read into the treaty.

In November 2013, the Madras High Court, in the case of Verizon Communications Singapore (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2013] 39 taxmann.com 70, ruled that the amount paid by Indian companies to a foreign company for dedicated broadband services constituted "royalty" and ought to be taxed in India under the Income-tax Act as well as the India Singapore treaty. Analyzing the technical aspects of providing bandwidth services in detail and interpreting the retrospective amendments to the definition of 'royalty' in section 9 made by Finance Act, 2012, the Madras High Court observed that the retrospective amendment had removed all doubts insofar as the expression 'use or right to use' was to be understood in the context of possession, control or location, thus approving that the term 'use or right to use' is of wide amplitude.

IBM and Sonata have now approached the Apex Court for determining whether packaged software can be taxed as royalty under DTAAs. It appears that only the verdict of the Supreme Court will put this debate to rest.

B. TRANSFER PRICING

Though transfer pricing is a relatively new area of law, we have all recently witnessed 2 high profile cases before the Bombay High Court that thrust the subject into limelight. Till a couple of years ago, only tax professionals dealing with international tax management/compliance of MNCs were concerned with the nuances of transfer pricing. However, there has been a noticeable change in this trend, with the print and electronic media reporting extensively on these cases. Suddenly, transfer pricing has become a topic of interest not only with most tax professionals but with the general public as well. The fact that transfer pricing has less to do with tax and more to do with market dynamics and economics definitely has a role to play in this development. But another, more important reason, for the increased interest in transfer pricing is the fact that most economies have started showing decreased tolerance to the practices adopted by MNCs for shifting profits to low tax jurisdictions, thereby depriving the "source countries" of their legitimate revenue. The vigour with which OECD is driving its Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) Action Plan and the frequency with which this problem is being discussed at international forums indicates the increasing concern of tax base erosion. Before I elaborate more on BEPS, I want to touch upon a few important issues that are currently in focus.

I. Vodafone II and Vodafone III before Bombay High Court

It seems that any litigation involving 'Vodafone' can never be a low-key affair. If foreign investors complained of flip flops on indirect share transfers in 2012, subjecting share issue transactions to transfer pricing provisions left them 'Shell Shocked' in 2013.

In a detailed judgment of 239 pages, the Bombay High Court cleared the air on some important procedural aspects in the realm of transfer pricing, including the powers of the AO, TPO and DRP. In this case popularly termed as "Vodafone II", the High Court clarified that the AO is not only bound by the TPO's decision in respect of ALP computation, but is also bound by the TPO's decision as regards the character of the transaction i.e. whether or not the transaction is an 'international transaction.' The High Court also held that the powers of the DRP are wide enough to consider all questions of fact/law raised before it. The DRP's power to 'confirm' a transfer pricing adjustment would also include the power 'not to confirm' the same, thereby empowering it to annul the variations as well.

Till now, the Tribunals have been holding that packaged software being ‘goods’, there was no need for the importer to deduct tax at source and that the payment towards procurement of the packaged software cannot be considered as ‘royalty’. However, this latest decision from the Karnataka High Court would supersede such Tribunals’ decisions, at least, for importers in Karnataka. 2.2 The facts of the case, in brief: Certain importers of software licenses had taken a view that the payments made for software imports would not attract the provisions of section 195 of the Income-tax Act, necessitating the deduction of tax at source, since such payments would not constitute taxable income in the nature of royalty or scientific work, in the hands of the non-resident, in terms of section 9(1)(vi) read with the DTAA. The First and Second Appellate Authorities had upheld the importers’ contention that when the payments would be for acquiring a right to use a copyright and not the copyright itself it would not get treated as royalty payments in terms of the DTAAs and, hence, there was no need for deducting tax at source under section 195. The Tribunal had also upheld the importers’ contention that the import of software licenses would be in the nature of a transaction involving import of goods, in the light of the precedents set by the various Courts including the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the TCS case. The revenue contended that software is a ‘scientific work’ and payments for import of software would be covered under section 9(1)(vi) of the Act and that the importer cannot contend that the payment made by him would not constitute income in the hands of the non-resident recipient and that, the importer is duty-bound to deduct tax at source under section 195.

2.3 The gist of the judgment: In a sweeping judgment, which is perhaps the first judgment from a High Court on the contentious issue related to the applicability of section 195 on software imports, the Karnataka High Court has rejected, in toto, the decisions of the Bangalore Tribunal in various similar judgments and has held that the importer was duty-bound to deduct tax at source under section 195 for import of software licenses, based almost exclusively, on the Apex Court’s judgment in Transmission Corporation of AP Ltd. v. CIT [1999] 105 Taxman 742. The High Court’s judgment in leads to the premise that the obligation to deduct tax at source under section 195 has nothing to do, with the actual liability of the non-resident to tax under the provisions of the Act, including the quantum thereof. The importer could take recourse to the provisions of section 195(2) if he is of the view that only a part of the payment made by him would bear the character of income in the hands of the non-resident.

2.4 The implications arising out of this judgment: Due to this ruling of the Karnataka High Court, all overseas payments will now be subject to withholding tax, whether or not the income is taxable. Not only is this in dramatic contrast to previous High Court’s decisions, it is also a judgment that will lead to higher cost of business, increased uncertainty and may be even more litigation—at Least for a while.

The law itself as it reads, which is section 195, specifically says that it is a sum which is chargeable to tax under the Income-tax Act on which tax has to be deducted at source, if that payment, of course, is being made to a non-resident. Based on that, for example, the Rajasthan High Court in the SBI case has taken a view that if income is exempt under provisions of the Indian Income-tax Act, one does not need to withhold tax at source at all when the payment is being made to non-resident of such an exempt income.

But now, a judgment by the Karnataka High Court has turned this established principle.

•In terms of this judgment, the importer has only two options before him, vis-à-vis the payments to be effected to the non-resident, viz. either to deduct tax at source under section 195 or to make an application to the Department under section 195(2). In terms of the judgment, this principle would apply equally to import of goods or to import of services or for transactions involving import of goods and services as in the case of a works contract.

•It would look like that importer cannot get into issues related to the applicability of section 9(1) or to the provisions of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements (DTAA) for purposes of discharging his liability under section 195. In other words, in terms of this judgment, the provisions of section 195 are quite draconian, requiring the resident payer to deduct tax at source without getting into issues related to the taxation of the receipts, in the hands of the non-resident.

Can additional amount be collected as ‘service tax’ on royalties and technical services? - The amount of tax that can be collected under DTAA is already collected by Government of India under income tax provisions. The question is whether some additional amount can be collected as ‘service tax’ on royalty and technical services? Article 2(2) of Convention very clearly states that the convention applies to any identical or substantially similar taxes which are imposed after convention.

Charging service tax on gross amount of technical services provided by non-resident seems to be nothing but additional tax by different name.

Collecting the tax from service receiver means doing something indirectly which you cannot do directly, as effect of both is same.

12.7 Services provided by person who has no place of business in India - Article 7 of the convention with USA reads as follows, ‘The profits of an enterprise of a Contracting State shall be taxable only in that State unless the enterprise carries on business in the other Contracting State through a permanent establishment situated therein. If the enterprise carries on business as aforesaid, the profits of the enterprise may be taxed in the other State but only so much of them as is attributable to (a) that permanent establishment ; (b) sales in the other State of goods or merchandise of the same or similar kind as those sold through that permanent establishment ; or (c) other business activities carried on in the other State of the same or similar kind as those effected through that permanent establishment’.

What cannot be directly, can as well not be done indirectly. It may be noted that a person providing service abroad cannot charge ‘service tax’ in his invoice to the service receiver.

For example, if Income Tax Act provides that amounts paid for services to non-resident will not be allowable as ‘expenditure’ under Income Tax Act, it will amount to imposing a tax on services provided by non-resident. Characterisation of income from software 12. The question as to whether consideration for transfer of computer software is royalty or business income or capital gains is a debatable question. Computer software means a computer programme recorded on any disc, tape, perforated media or other information storage device. It is a programme which contains instructions to the computer. Software is usually developed in three stages. First, a systematic analyst or designer prepares a specification, which normally includes data flow diagrams setting out the basic logic of the programme. Then a source code programme is written in computer language. The source code cannot be read directly by a computer. It is converted by an assembler or compiler into object code. Object code is essentially a form of source code which can be read or relied upon by microprocessor or Central Processor Unit (CPU) of the computer. Authorship of source code or the object code is protected by Copyright Act, as library work. Whether consideration involved in the transaction of software is business or service income or royalty depends upon transfer of the rights therein. Predominant amongst the considerations is whether the transferor has received not only the right to use the software in its business, but also the right to reproduce and redistribute the software to others. The rights transferred are: (1) less than all the rights; (2) outright alienation; or (3) mixture of both. Transaction in (1) above may yield business or royalty income depending on how the rights are transferred. It is the business income when the transfer is made for the personal or business use of the acquirer, on terms which make the acquisition anytheless than the full rights in the software. The owner still preserves copyright protection and restricts his acquirers use of the software. It is a transfer of the copyrighted article rather than the copyright itself. It is royalty income when the payment is received for a partial transfer of rights. Such transaction involves granting of licence to the other party to develop and market the software commercially, in the same manner as the author of a book grants rights to a publisher. However, if the transactions involve the disposition of the entire right such as an exclusive geographical licence for the useful life of the software, the income is not royalty. It is a sale of the copyright itself in a book. Such transactions involve outright alienation. Thus, transfer of a software is a sale of product (transfer of a standard form) like a copyrighted article; sale of copyright, or by way of grant of licence to develop and market commercially.

Transfer of a software is a sale of product (transfer of a standard form) like a copyrighted article; sale of copyright, or by way of grant of licence to develop and market commercially.

When the software payments are made under the mixed contracts (e.g. as part of a package or bundled scheme of payments for computer operated machine) then it would be necessary to break the payment units to be treated as royalty or business income or capital gains [for detailed discussion, see D.P. Mittal’s Indian Double Taxation Agreements, published by Taxmann, 4th Edn. (2004)]. I. Introduction

The Supreme Court of India, in its recent pronouncement in Hyatt International Southwest Asia Ltd.[2025] 176 taxmann.com 783 (SC), has delivered a vital ruling affirming the existence of its Permanent Establishment (PE) in India. This judgment goes beyond a mere case-specific outcome. It provides a crucial clarification on the "fixed place of business" PE concept, particularly for service-oriented multinational corporations.

The ruling reinforces the Indian judiciary's stance on substance over form in international taxation, building upon established precedents. The core question before the Supreme Court was whether Hyatt International Southwest Asia Ltd., a UAE-based company, had a Permanent Establishment in India under Article 5(1) of the Indo-UAE DTAA, and consequently, whether its income derived from Strategic Oversight Services Agreements (SOSAs) was taxable in India.

II. Background of the Dispute

The appellant in this case, Hyatt International Southwest Asia Ltd., is a company incorporated in the UAE and recognised as a tax resident of the UAE under Article 4 of the Agreement between the Government of India and the UAE for the Avoidance of Double Taxation (DTAA).

The core of the dispute originated in the year 2008, when the appellant entered into two Strategic Oversight Services Agreements (SOSAs) with Asian Hotels Limited (AHL), a company based in India. These agreements pertained to the operation of hotels in Delhi and Mumbai. Under the SOSAs, Hyatt International Southwest Asia Ltd. committed to providing strategic planning services and "know-how" to ensure the hotels were developed and operated as efficient, high-quality international full-service establishments. These agreements were notably long-term, stipulating a twenty-year term from the effective date, with a provision for extension by an additional ten years through mutual agreement.

The dispute spanned multiple assessment years. For the Assessment Year 2009-10, the appellant filed its return declaring 'Nil' income and claiming a refund. Following scrutiny, the Assessing Officer (AO) held that the appellant's activities constituted a business connection under Section 9(1)(i) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, and a Permanent Establishment (PE) under Article 5 of the DTAA.

The matter reached the Delhi High Court, and the High Court concluded that Hyatt International Southwest Asia Ltd., despite being a Dubai-incorporated and UAE tax-resident company, indeed had a Permanent Establishment in India in the form of a fixed place of business. Dissatisfied with this finding on the existence of a PE, Hyatt International Southwest Asia Ltd. subsequently appealed to the Supreme Court of India.

III. Legal Framework: Permanent Establishment under the India-UAE DTAA

The concept of 'Permanent Establishment' is foundational in international tax law, serving as the threshold for a source state to tax the business profits of a foreign enterprise. Under Article 5(1) of the India-UAE DTAA, a PE is defined as "a fixed place of business through which the business of an enterprise is wholly or partly carried on". This definition is consistent with Section 92F(iiia) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. It aligns with international models such as the UN Model Double Taxation Convention and the OECD Model Tax Convention. This fundamental definition requires both a stable physical location and business activity conducted through it.

The Supreme Court, relying heavily on its precedent in Formula One World Championship Limited [2017] 80 taxmann.com 347 (SC), has emphasised two essential conditions for a fixed place PE:

(i)

The place must be "at the disposal" of the enterprise, and

(ii)

The business of the enterprise must be carried on through that place.

Furthermore, a PE must demonstrate three core attributes: stability (an enduring or permanent nature of presence), productivity (the place must be used to carry on productive business activities), and dependence (the personnel conducting the business at the fixed place are dependent on the enterprise).

The "disposal test" is considered pivotal, implying a right to use and control the premises for the enterprise's own business activities.

The Court emphasised the "disposal test" and its contextual application signals an adaptation to modern, often asset-light, business models. In an era where physical presence might be minimal, such as through remote management or cloud-based services, but operational control remains pervasive, traditional notions of "fixed place" are challenged. By focusing on the right to use and control premises for the enterprise's own business, even without ownership or exclusive possession, the Court ensures that economic nexus and the ability to generate profits from a location, rather than merely a physical footprint, form the basis for taxation.

UN MODEL OF TREATIES

5. Article 7 of the U.N. Model Convention, inter alia, provides that only that portion of business profits is taxable in the source country which is attributable to the PE. It specifies how such business profits should be ascertained. Under the said article, a PE is treated as if it is an independent enterprise (profit centre) de hors the head office and which deals with the head office at arm’s length. Therefore, its profits are determined on the basis as if it is an independent enterprise. The profits of the PE are determined on the basis of what an independent enterprise under similar circumstances might be expected to derive on its own. Article 7(2) of the U.N. Model Convention advocates the arm’s length approach for attribution of profits to a PE.

The object behind enactment of transfer pricing regulations is to prevent shifting of profits outside India. Under article 7(2) not all profits of MSCo would be taxable in India but only those which have economic nexus with the PE in India. A foreign enterprise is liable to be taxed in India on so much of its business profit as is attributable to its PE in India. The quantum of taxable income is to be determined in accordance with the provisions of the Act. All provisions of the Act are applicable, including provisions relating to depreciation, investment losses, deductible expenses, carry-forward and set-off losses, etc.

The Apex Court did refer to article 7 of the Indo-US treaty in para 7, but decided the question of ‘attribution of profits’, on the basis of the UN model. There is important difference between para 2 in the US treaty and the UN model. The additional sentence in the Indo-US treaty is reproduced below:

‘’...and other enterprises controlling, controlled by or subject to the same common control as the enterprise. In any case where the correct amount of profits attributable to a permanent establishment is incapable of determination or the determination thereof presents exceptional difficulties, the profits attributable to the permanent establishment may be estimated on a reasonable basis. The estimate adopted shall, however, be such that the result shall be in accordance with the principles contained in this Article’’. (p. 178)

The common part of para is also reproduced below:

"Subject to the provisions of paragraph 3, where an enterprise of a Contracting State carries on business in the other Contracting State through a permanent establishment situated therein, there shall in each Contracting State be attributed to that permanent establishment the profits which it might be expected to make if it were a distinct and independent enterprise engaged in the same or similar activities under the same or similar conditions and dealing wholly at arm’s length with the enterprise of which it is a permanent establishment...."

However, it is possible that the non-resident entity may have a business connection with the resident Indian entity. In such a case, the resident Indian entity could be treated as the Permanent Establishment of the non-resident entity. The tax treatment of the Permanent Establishment in such a case is under consideration in this circular. During the last decade or so, India has seen a steady growth of outsourcing of business processes by non-residents or foreign companies to IT-enabled entities in India. Such entities are either branches or associated enterprises of the foreign enterprise or an independent Indian enterprise. Their activities range from mere procurement of orders for sale of goods or provision of services and answering sales related queries, to the provision of services itself like software maintenance service, debt collection service, software development service, credit card/mobile telephone related service, etc. The non-resident entity or the foreign company will be liable to tax in India only if the IT-enabled BPO unit in India constitutes its Permanent Establishment. The extent to which the profit of the non-resident enterprise is to be attributed to the activities of such Permanent Establishment in India has been under consideration of the Board.

A non-resident or a foreign company is treated as having a Permanent Establishment in India under Article 5 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements entered into by India with different countries if the said non-resident or foreign company carries on business in India through a branch, sales office etc. or through an agent (other than an independent agent) who habitually exercises an authority to conclude contracts or regularly delivers goods or merchandise or habitually secures orders on behalf of the non-resident principal. In such a case, the profits of the non-resident or foreign company attributable to the business activities carried out in India by the Permanent Establishment become taxable in India under Article 7 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement.

Paragraph 1 of Article 7 of Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements provides that if a foreign enterprise carries on business in another country through a Permanent Establishment situated therein, the profits of the enterprise may be taxed in the other country but only so much of them as are attributable to the Permanent Establishment. Paragraph 2 of the same Article provides that subject to the provisions of Paragraph 3, there shall in each contracting State be attributed to that Permanent Establishment the profits which it might be expected to make if it were a distinct and separate enterprise engaged in the same or similar activities under the same or similar conditions and dealing wholly independently with the enterprise of which it is a Permanent Establishment. Paragraph 3 of the Article provides that in determining the profits of a Permanent Establishment there shall be allowed as deduction expenses which are incurred for the purposes of the Permanent Establishment including executive and general administrative expenses so incurred, whether in the State in which the Permanent Establishment is situated or elsewhere. What are the expenses that are deductible would have to be determined in accordance with the accepted principles of accountancy and the provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961.

Paragraph 2 contains the central directive on which the allocation of profits to a Permanent Establishment is intended to be based. The paragraph incorporates the view that the profits to be attributed to a Permanent Establishment are those which that Permanent Establishment would have made if, instead of dealing with its Head Office, it had been dealing with an entirely separate enterprise under conditions and at prices prevailing in the ordinary market. This corresponds to the "arm’s length principle". Paragraph 3 only provides a rule applicable for the determination of the profits of the Permanent Establishment, while paragraph 2 requires that the profits so determined correspond to the profits that a separate and independent enterprise would have made. Hence, in determining the profits attributable to an IT-enabled BPO unit constituting a Permanent Establishment, it will be necessary to determine the price of the services rendered by the Permanent Establishment to the Head Office or by the Head Office to the Permanent Establishment on the basis of "arm’s length principle".

"Arm’s length price" would have the same meaning as in the definition in section 92F(iii) of the Income-tax Act. The arm’s length price would have to be determined in accordance with the provisions of sections 92 to 92F of the Act.

The CBDT Circular No. 1/2004, dated 2nd January, 2004 is hereby withdrawn with immediate effect.

CONCEPT OF PERMANENT ESTABLISHMENT

5. The concept of PE was introduced into the Income-tax Act, 1961 as part of the statutory provisions of transfer pricing by the Finance Act, 2001. In section 92F(iii), the word ‘enterprise’ is defined to mean ‘a person including a PE of such person who is proposed to be engaged in any activity relating to the production’. The CBDT Circular No. 14 of 2001 has clarified that the term P.E. has not been defined in the Act, but its meaning may be understood with reference to the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) entered into by India. The article 5 of the DTAA1 4, which India enters into with other countries, lays down that ‘a permanent establishment means a fixed place of business through which the business of an enterprise is wholly or partly carried on’. Thus, the intention was to rely upon the concept and definition of PE in the DTAA.

However, vide the Finance Act, 2002 the definition of PE was inserted in the Income-tax Act, 1961 vide section 92F (iiia) which states that the PE shall include a fixed place of business through which the business of the Multi National Enterprise (MNE) is wholly or partly carried on. The difference lies therein between the definition of the word ‘PE’ in the inclusive sense under the Income-tax Act as against the definition of the word ‘PE’ in the exhaustive sense under the DTAA. This analysis is important because it indicates the intention of the Parliament in adopting an inclusive definition of PE so as to cover all forms of PE inclusive of service PE, agency PE, software PE, Construction PE, etc.

In a ruling given by the Authority for Advance Rulings, India (‘AAR’), the AAR has held that a subsidiary may be regarded as a PE, if it does not have significant independent activities of its own.15 In another ruling, the AAR has held that if the agent does not have the authority to conclude contract, then he cannot constitute a PE16 . However, on the other hand, if the parent executes mass contracts made on standard forms without being scrutinized by it, then the agent may constitute a PE. The Supreme Court of India in DIT (International Taxation) v. Morgan Stanley & Co. Inc.1 7 [2007] 162 Taxman 165 has gone a long way in demystifying the concept of permanent establishment in India.

The AAR delivered following ruling as:—

u The applicant cannot be regarded as having a fixed place of business under article 5(1)18 of the DTAA as although it has a place of business in India, yet the same was constituted to perform back office functions and under article 5(3)(e) which begins with a non obstante clause, such functions which are of a preparatory or auxiliary nature do not constitute a PE. adaptation to modern, often asset-light, business models. In an era where physical presence might be minimal, such as through remote management or cloud-based services, but operational control remains pervasive, traditional notions of "fixed place" are challenged. By focusing on the right to use and control premises for the enterprise's own business, even without ownership or exclusive possession, the Court ensures that economic nexus and the ability to generate profits from a location, rather than merely a physical footprint, form the basis for taxation. This approach provides a robust framework for taxing profits from cross-border digital services or remote management arrangements, even if a traditional physical office is not maintained. It suggests that Indian tax authorities are prepared to look beyond formal structures to identify substantive economic activity and assert taxing rights, aligning with global efforts to address base erosion and profit shifting.

Article 5(2) of the DTAA provides an inclusive list of what constitutes a PE, such as a place of management, branch, office, factory, workshop, mine, or farm. Crucially for service-oriented businesses, Article 5(2)(i) specifically includes "the furnishing of services including consultancy services by an enterprise... through employees or other personnel... provided that such activities continue for the same project or connected project for a period or periods aggregating more than 9 months within any twelve-month period". This clause addresses service PEs based on the duration of personnel presence.

The appellant in this case explicitly argued that its employee presence did not exceed the 9-month threshold under Article 5(2)(i). While the Court addressed this by clarifying that "continuity of business presence in aggregate" is the relevant consideration, its primary finding was that of a fixed place of business under the more general Article 5(1).

This indicates that even if the specific service PE conditions, such as the time threshold for individual personnel, are not met, a broader fixed place PE can still be established if the enterprise exercises pervasive control over a location where its core business is conducted. This implies that Article 5(1) acts as a wider net, capable of catching arrangements that might slip through the more specific conditions of 5(2).

The Court's reasoning implies that pervasive control and deep functional involvement (leading to a 5(1) PE) are often more determinative than the mere duration of individual employee visits (which is relevant for 5(2)(i)). The underlying principle is that the nature and extent of the contractual relationship and actual operational control over a fixed place can establish a PE, irrespective of whether the service PE duration test is met for every single employee. This compels companies to consider their overall operational footprint and control, not just individual travel logs.

IV. Appellant's Arguments

Hyatt International vehemently contended that it did not have a Permanent Establishment in India, asserting several key points to challenge the High Court's findings.

A primary contention revolved around the absence of a fixed place of business or office in India. The appellant submitted that there was no designated space or office at the hotel premises in Delhi or Mumbai that was specifically reserved for or placed at its disposal. It claimed to exercise no control or dominion over any part of the premises.

Furthermore, the appellant argued that the limited and occasional presence of its employees in India did not exceed the nine-month threshold stipulated under Article 5(2)(i) of the DTAA, thereby precluding the existence of a service PE. It emphasised that these visits were brief, routine, spread across multiple locations, and lacked exclusive use or control over any space.

The appellant contended that the High Court erroneously disregarded two essential conditions for a fixed place of business PE as laid down in Formula One and E-Funds: (a) the necessity of a specific, fixed, and identifiable physical location in India; and (b) that such location must be at the disposal of the foreign enterprise for use in carrying out its own business activities.

It was also argued that the appellant's role under the SOSA was limited to providing strategic guidance, ensuring brand compliance, and developing long-term plans. The appellant maintained that Hyatt India Pvt. Ltd. managed the day-to-day operations of the hotel under a separate Hotel Operating Services Agreement (HOSA), and that the appellant was not involved in this daily management.

Finally, the appellant submitted that the High Court incorrectly inferred a right of disposal from the mere absence of an express prohibition in the SOSA on decision-making by the appellant's employees during their stay. It was argued that a fixed place of business PE cannot be presumed from the absence of a restriction; rather, there must be an affirmative grant of a right to use a specific physical location to carry on the enterprise's own business.

V. Supreme Court's Analysis

The Supreme Court meticulously reviewed the Strategic Oversight Services Agreement (SOSA), concluding that the appellant's role "was not confined to mere policy formulation" but conferred upon it a "continuing and enforceable right to implement its policies and ensure compliance in all operational aspects of the hotel". This degree of control and supervision, the Court held, "clearly transcends a mere advisory capacity and aligns with the criteria for a Fixed Place Permanent Establishment (PE) under Article 5(1) of the India - UAE DTAA".

The customized software means software developed for a specific customer to meet his specific requirements. The software industry prior to the introduction of new category of taxable service in the name of 'Information Technology Software Service' was at an advantageous position, as no indirect taxes were applicable on the development of customized software treating it as a service contract. However, the advantageous position got diluted after the introduction of new category as above, as now development of customized software attracts service tax. The dilution has further been deepened after the judgment of the Hon'ble Madras High Court in the case of Infosys Technologies Ltd. in which it has been held that even customized software may qualify as goods.

The sales tax authorities after taking recourse to the judgment of the Hon'ble Madras High Court are issuing notices demanding tax on the transaction involving development of software. The judgment has opened a Pandora's Box of litigations in relation to customized/uncanned software.

Another area of litigation concerning software is supply of software through electronic downloads. In such a scenario, service tax gets attracted in view of the specific language of the taxable service under the category of 'Information Technology Software Service'. However, whether sales tax is also payable is another point where litigation surrounds the software industry. The Hon'ble Karnataka High Court recently in the case of Sasken Communication Technologies Ltd. has observed that intellectual property once put on a medium becomes goods and when transferred is leviable to sales tax. After this judgment, the industry players can hope that the sales tax authorities do not litigate on this issue.

The menace of double taxation is detrimental to the interests of users of goods/services as it results into high procurement costs, especially in those cases where credit of input taxes paid cannot be taken by the users. The domestic users only take a hit as the exporters of software generally enjoy the tax free status and, accordingly, no taxes are charged on the value of goods/services exported from India. Presently, the sales tax (local VAT) rate for software is either at 4% or at 5% and service tax rate is at 10%, which can significantly enhance the costs of procurements in case software suffers double taxation, specifically in cases where the credit of input taxes is not available either in full or in part.

Though the laws on sales tax and service tax are on the statute books for good number of years now, yet the provisions of these laws need alignment, which seems to be an uphill task in view of the fact that the Governments desire to garner more and more revenue and sometimes it happens by introducing provisions which put the taxpayer in a situation where he has no alternative but to resort to litigation.

One of the group companies of Morgan Stanley, Morgan Stanley Advantages Services (P.) Ltd. (‘MSAS’) entered into an agreement for providing certain support services to MSCo. On May 19, 2005, MSCo. (Applicant) filed an advance ruling application in Form 34-C inviting its advance ruling on several points. The basic question relating to the transaction between the applicant and MSAS on which advance ruling was sought was two fold, namely, whether the applicant was having a PE in India under article 5(1) of the DTAA on account of the services rendered by MSAS under the Services Agreement dated April 14, 2005 entered into by MSAS with the applicant? And if so, what was the amount of income attributable to such PE?

By the impugned ruling delivered on February 13, 2006 by the Authority for Advance Ruling (‘AAR’), it was held, inter alia, that the applicant cannot be regarded as having a fixed place of business PE under article 5(1); that MSAS cannot be regarded as an agency PE under article 5(4); and that the applicant would be regarded as having a PE in India under article 5(2)(1) if it were to send some of its employees to India as stewards or as deputationists in the employment of MSAS.

Against this ruling of the AAR, the applicant (against the observation that the MSCo. will be said to have an agency PE in India if it were to send some of its employees to India as stewards in the employment of MSAS) and the Department (against the observation that MSAS cannot be said to be a fixed PE of MSCo. in India) approached the Supreme Court in appeal by way of special leave petition.

According to the Department, the applicant should be regarded as having a fixed place in India under article 5(1) as the applicant proposes to carry on its business through MSAS in India. According to the Department, MSAS was the PE of the MSCo. in India. They had a fixed place of business in Mumbai. According to the Department, the nature of the activities proposed to be performed by MSAS in Mumbai indicated that the said company represented the business presence of the MSCo. in India. The Department also submitted that MSAS was legally and financially dependent upon the applicant and, consequently, MSAS constituted an agency PE of the applicant under article 5(4).

Both these contentions were rejected by the AAR vide the above impugned ruling. On the second question, the AAR ruled that the Transactional Net Margin Method (TNMM) was the most appropriate method for the determination of the Arm’s Length Price (ALP) in respect of the service agreement dated April 14, 2005 between the applicant and the MSAS and as the said method meets the test of arm’s length as prescribed under section 92C of the 1961 Act, no further income was attributable in the hands of MSAS in India. The Supreme Court ruled in Director of Income-tax (International Taxation) v. Morgan Stanley & Co. Inc. [2007] 162 Taxman 165 that Morgan Stanley had used the correct transfer pricing method to determine payments to MSAS, one of its group companies incorporated in India, and that no further income could be attributed to the PE. It observed that the relationship or ‘economic nexus’ between companies is important in determining taxability. In each case, the data placed by the taxpayer has to be examined as to whether the transfer pricing analysis placed by the taxpayer is exhaustive of attribution of profits and that would depend on the functional and factual analysis to be undertaken in each case. In this article, the author analyzes the Supreme Court’s decision against the background of the U.S. tax treaty and the U.N. Model Convention. The author submits that certain provisions of US treaty escaped the attention of the Apex Court, in the absence of those being brought to the Hon’ble Court’s kind notice. Since the law laid down by the Supreme Court would have far reaching effect on the cases already decided and future cases, an urgent review of the decision may meet the interest of justice.

INTRODUCTION

1. The Supreme Court ruled in Director of Income-tax (International Taxation) v. Morgan Stanley [2007] 162 Taxman 165 that Morgan Stanley had used the correct transfer pricing method to determine payments to Morgan Stanley Advantage Services Private Ltd. (MSAS), one of its group companies incorporated in India, and that no further income could be attributed to the PE. It observed that the relationship or ‘economic nexus’ between companies was important in determining taxability. Under the impugned ruling delivered by the AAR, remuneration to MSAS was justified by a transfer pricing analysis and, therefore, no further income could be attributed to the PE (MSAS). In other words, the said ruling equates an arm’s length analysis (ALA) with attribution of profits. It holds that once a transfer pricing analysis is undertaken, there is no further need to attribute profits to a PE. The impugned ruling is correct in principle insofar as an associated enterprise, that also constitutes a PE, has been remunerated on an arm’s length basis taking into account all the risk-taking functions of the enterprise. In such cases nothing further would be left to be attributed to the PE. The situation would be different if transfer pricing analysis does not adequately reflect the functions performed and the risks assumed by the enterprise. In such a situation, there would be a need to attribute profits to the PE for those functions/risks that have not been considered. Therefore, in each case, the data placed by the taxpayer has to be examined as to whether the transfer pricing analysis placed by the taxpayer is exhaustive of attribution of profits and that would depend on the functional and factual analysis to be undertaken in each case. Lastly, it may be added that taxing corporates on the basis of the concept of economic nexus is an important feature of attributable profits (profits attributable to the PE).

2. Taxability of ‘profits’ and ‘attribution of profits’ have to be done under paras 1 and 2 of article 7 of DTAA. Para 1 deals with the quantum of profits of the PE and para 2 with ‘attribution of profits’ to the PE. For arriving at the conclusion, the Supreme Court referred to para 1, as under:

"para 16 under article 7, the taxability is of the MNE. What is to be taxed under article 7 is income of the MNE attributable to the P.E. in India. The income attributable to the said P.E. is the income attributable to foreign company’s operations in India, which in turn, implies the income attributable to the activities carried on by the MNE through its P.E. in India. Therefore, there is a difference between the taxability of the P.E. in respect of its income earned by it in India which is in accordance with the Income-tax Act and which has nothing to do with the taxability of the MNE, which is also taxable in India under article 7, in respect of the profits attributable to its P.E. Under article 7, the taxability is of the MNE. What is taxable under article 7 is profits earned by the MNE. Under the said Income-tax Act, the taxable unit is the foreign company, though the quantum of income taxable is income attributable to the P.E. of the said foreign company in India." (p. 181)

A deals with the concept of income deemed to accrue or arise in India. section 9(1)(i) of the ITA deals with the concept of business connection which states that all income accrue or arise through or from any business connection in India is deemed to accrue or arise in India and taxable under the provisions of the ITA. However, the term 'business connection' is not defined under the ITA. The Hon'ble SC has defined the business connection in detail. On the other hand, under the DTAA, business profits are taxable in India only if such taxpayer has PE11 in India. Further, unlike domestic law, the term PE is defined under Article 5 of the DTAA.

On comparison of two term business connection and PE, it can be understood that the term business connection is much wider in scope than PE. Which means that existence of PE always gives arise to business connection in India.

However, existence of business connection may or may not result in PE in India. Accordingly, there may be situations wherein the taxpayer may have a business connection India but not PE. In such a scenario, business profits are not taxable in India as there is not PE in India.

Scope of income viz. dividend, interest or royalty/FTS under ITA vs DTAA:

Under domestic law, fees for technical services is taxable under section 9(1)(vii) of the ITA which provides detailed definition for the term 'fees for technical services'. However, under the DTAA, such an income is taxable under Article 12. Article 12 of the DTAA provides a narrow definition for the term 'fees for technical services'.

The judicial fora in India including the Hon'ble SC on many occasions have held that while determining whether a particular income covered under the definition of 'fees for technical services', provisions of DTAA shall prevail over the provisions of the ITA.

For example, treaties entered into by the India with some countries viz. Canada, Netherlands, Portugal, UK, USA etc., the term fees for technical services does not include 'managerial service' though the same is included in the provisions of domestic law.

Further, DTAA entered into by India with some countries viz. Canada, Netherlands, Portugal, Singapore, UK, USA etc., services provided by the assessee is treated as fees for technical services only if such services satisfy the 'make available' test12.

In the above situations, the judicial fora have held that, though the services are covered under the definition of 'fees for technical services' under the domestic law, as such services are not covered under the DTAA, payment made for services are not taxable in the source country. This is because the provisions of DTAA overrides the provisions of domestic law.

Similarly, section 9(1) (vi) of the ITA deals with the definition of royalty and the scope of royalty is much wider than the definition contained in Article 12 of the DTAA. Applying the same ratio, taxpayer may not be taxed in India as the transaction entered by the taxpayer may not fall under the definition of royalty under the DTAA though the same is treated as royalty under section 9(1) (vi) of the ITA.

Rate of Tax under ITA vs. DTAA:

As per the provisions of ITA, income tax payable by the taxpayer shall be increased by applicable surcharge and cess. For example, section 115A of the ITA states that FTS is taxable at the rate of 10 percent. However, such rate of 10 percent under section 115A shall be increased by surcharge at the applicable rates and cess of 4 percent. On the other hand, Article 12 of DTAA13 states that FTS earned in India is taxable at the rate of 10 percent.

However, DTAA does not contain any provision which states that such rate of tax shall be increased by surcharge and cess. In this regard, the question arises is whether the taxpayer, when rate of tax as per DTAA is considered, is required include the surcharge and cess while computing the tax payable.

The Kolkata Tribunal in the case of DIC Asia Pacific Pte. Ltd.14 v. Asstt. DIT (International Taxation) has held that 'the provisions of Articles 11 and 12 must find precedence over the provisions of the Income Tax Act and restrict the taxability, whether in respect of income tax or surcharge or additional surcharge – whatever name called, at the rates specified in the respective article. In any case, education cess was introduced by the Finance Act 2004, with effect from assessment year 2005-06 which was much after the signing of India Singapore tax DTAA on 24th January 1994. In view of the specific provisions to the effect that the scope of Article 2 shall also cover "any identical or substantially similar taxes which are imposed by either Contracting State after the date of signature of the present Agreement in addition to, or in place of, the taxes referred to in paragraph 1", and in view of the fact that education cess is essentially of the same nature as surcharge, being an additional surcharge, the scope of article 2 also extends to the education cess.'

Such royalties and fees for ‘included services’ may also be taxed in the Contracting State in which they arise and according to the laws of that State; but such tax on gross amount cannot exceed 15% of ‘gross amount’. It may be noted that this amount is already collected as TDS under Income-tax provisions.

Can additional amount be collected as ‘service tax’ on royalties and technical services? - The amount of tax that can be collected under DTAA is already collected by Government of India under income-tax provisions. The question is whether some additional amount can be collected as ‘service tax’ on royalty and technical services? Article 2(2) of Convention very clearly states that the convention applies to any identical or substantially similar taxes which are imposed after Convention.

Charging service tax on gross amount of technical services provided by non-resident seems to be nothing but additional tax by different name.

Collecting the tax from service receiver means doing something indirectly which you cannot do directly, as effect of both is same.

9.3 Services provided by person who has no place of business in India - Article 7 of the Convention with USA reads as follows:

‘The profits of an enterprise of a Contracting State shall be taxable only in that State unless the enterprise carries on business in the other Contracting State through a permanent establishment situated therein. If the enterprise carries on business as aforesaid, the profits of the enterprise may be taxed in the other State but only so much of them as is attributable to (a) that permanent establishment; (b) sales in the other State of goods or merchandise of the same or similar kind as those sold through that permanent establishment ; or (c) other business activities carried on in the other State of the same or similar kind as those effected through that permanent establishment’.

Article 7(1) of Convention with UK reads as follows:

‘The profits of an enterprise of a Contracting State shall be taxable only in that State unless the enterprise carries on business in the other Contracting State through a permanent establishment situated therein. If the enterprise carries on business as aforesaid, the profits of the enterprise may be taxed in the other State but only so much of them as is directly or indirectly attributable to that permanent establishment’. [identical provision in Convention with China and many other countries].

Charging service tax on service provided by non-resident amounts to tax on ‘profits’ - Charging service tax on services provided by person who has no place of business in India means indirectly taxing ‘profits’ of non-resident. What cannot be directly, can as well not be done indirectly. As explained above, only the liability of payment of service tax has been shifted to service receiver in respect of services received from a non-resident. It may be noted that a person providing service abroad cannot charge ‘service tax’ in his invoice to the service receiver.

For example, if Income-tax Act provides that amounts paid for services to non-resident will not be allowable as ‘expenditure’ under Income-tax Act, it will amount to imposing a tax on services provided by non-resident. This would be the easiest way of getting over restrictions placed under DTA agreements.

9.4 Conclusion - Charging service tax on services provided by person who does not have place of business in India amounts to indirectly imposing a tax on his income. What cannot be done directly can also not be done indirectly. It can be argued that in view of DTAA, service tax cannot be levied on services provided by person who does not have place of business in India. This is particularly so in case of royalty and technical services, for which specific provisions exist in DTAA.

3. Of late, the outsourcing industry around the world has been confronted with the contentious question of whether outsourced services provided by companies — particularly by captive service providers/manufacturers — would lead to a Permanent Establishment (PE) of the non-resident service recipient to come into existence under the terms of the relevant tax treaty. India has been a major beneficiary in the outsourcing boom, and, hence, if Indian tax authorities were to hold that such activities are tantamount to a PE, the global profits attributable to the PE would be taxable in India at the rate of 42.23 per cent7. Further, the availability of a tax credit in the home jurisdiction for such tax paid in India would be uncertain, potentially leading to double taxation and wiping out the economic advantage of outsourcing to India. On the other hand, if no PE exists, no profits can be subjected to Indian corporate tax.

In India, tax liability is based on the structure of the outsourcing contract and the scope of activities being undertaken. The generally preferred models, like third-party service providers, captive centres set up as wholly owned subsidiaries or outsourcing to transition partners on a BOT basis are taxed differently under Indian tax laws. Companies establishing captive facilities and BOT arrangements have to consider issues relating to transfer pricing and permanent establishment.

The Court explicitly rejected the appellant's argument that the absence of an exclusive or designated physical space within the hotel precluded a PE, reiterating Formula One's principle that "exclusive possession is not essential; temporary or shared use of space is sufficient, provided business is carried on through that space".

This demonstrates that the "fixed" element of a PE is about the enduring nature of the business activity and the right to use a location for that activity, rather than strict physical permanence or exclusivity of the foreign entity's own dedicated space. The 20-year contract term strongly reinforces the "stability" aspect, even if the physical space is not owned or leased exclusively. This has significant implications for businesses operating through shared facilities, co-working spaces, or through extensive contractual control over third-party premises.

The argument that the absence of an express prohibition on decision-making implied a right of disposal was also dismissed, with the Court emphasising that the test is one of "substance," meaning there must be an affirmative grant of a right to use a specific physical location to carry on the enterprise's own business.

The Supreme Court found that the appellant's activities fulfilled the three core attributes of a PE:

Stability: The 20-year duration of the SOSA, with a possibility of extension by ten years, clearly established the enduring nature and stability required for a PE. This long-term commitment signified a continuous and fixed presence.

Productivity: The appellant's entitlement to "Strategic Fees" was not a fixed fee but was calculated as a percentage of room revenue, other revenues, and cumulative gross operating profit. This profit-linked remuneration structure demonstrated an "active commercial involvement, linking the assessee's income to the financial and operational performance of the hotel," thereby satisfying the productivity test. The appellant's income was directly tied to the operational success of the hotel.

Dependence: The pervasive control exercised by the appellant over strategic, operational, and financial aspects, including staffing and policy formulation, indicated a strong dependence on the hotel's infrastructure and staff to carry out its business. The Court found the functions performed by the appellant's staff operating from the hotel premises to be "core and essential functions," not merely "auxiliary," clearly establishing their control over the day-to-day operations of the hotel.

The Court meticulously distinguished the Hyatt International case from precedents cited by the appellant:

E-Funds IT Solutions Inc. : The Court distinguished E-Funds [2017] 86 taxmann.com 240 (SC), where the Indian subsidiary merely provided "back-office support" and was compensated on an arm's length basis, with "no involvement in core business functions." In stark contrast, for Hyatt, "the hotel itself was the situs of the appellant's primary business operations, carried out under its direct supervision and aligned with its commercial interests." This distinction underscored that Hyatt's activities were central to the hotel's revenue generation and operational success, not merely supportive.

U.A.E Exchange Centre : Similarly, the Court clarified that Hyatt's activities "cannot be said that they were performing merely 'auxiliary' functions". In U.A.E Exchange Centre[2020] 116 taxmann.com 379 (SC), the liaison offices (LOs) in India performed only "preparatory and auxiliary activities," such as downloading information and dispatching cheques, without disposal rights over a fixed place for core business. Hyatt's pervasive control and direct involvement in management, human resources, marketing, and financial policies clearly surpassed such preparatory or auxiliary roles.

The Court's detailed analysis of the SOSA clauses and its explicit distinction from E-Funds and UAE Exchange Centre reveals that the "preparatory or auxiliary" exception (Article 5(3)(e)) is not a simple binary. Instead, it operates on a spectrum where activities that directly contribute to the primary revenue-generating operations of the local entity, especially when linked to profit-sharing or pervasive control, move from "auxiliary" to "core." The degree of integration, control, and direct impact on the local entity's profitability becomes the determinant. This nuanced interpretation means that foreign companies cannot simply label their activities as "advisory" or "supportive" to avoid PE. The tax authorities and courts will conduct a deep functional analysis of the activities, the extent of control exercised, and the remuneration structure to ascertain their true character. This places a higher burden on companies to demonstrate that their activities are genuinely peripheral to the local entity's core business.

The Court dismissed the appellant's submission that daily operations handled by Hyatt India Pvt. Ltd., a separate legal entity, negated the existence of a PE. It affirmed the well-established principle that "legal form does not override economic substance in determining PE status," emphasising the appellant's extent of control, strategic decision-making, and influence, which clearly established that business was carried on through the hotel premises.

A place qualifies if it is fixed through which business is, whether wholly or partly, carried on. It generally takes the form of a branch, an office, facility, a construction or an agency relationship, but does not include storage facilities, the maintenance of inventory, a facility simply for the purchase of goods, or any activity of a preparatory or auxiliary nature. A person is deemed PE if he is acting for the foreign enterprise and has the authority to conclude contracts (other than purchase contracts) or habitually exercises this authority. Such are dependent agents. Agents of independent status ailing in the ordinary course of their business are excluded. Mere agency for acting on behalf of a foreign enterprise is not enough. For the purposes of PE the agent must fill orders from a stock of goods or habitually exercise an authority to conclude contracts on behalf of or in the name of this foreign enterprise.

9.1 BPO Entity - Taxability "Attribution rule" - A non-resident or a foreign company is treated as having a permanent establishment or business connection in India under article 5 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements or under section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, if the said non-resident or foreign company carries on business in India through a branch, sales office etc., or through an agent (other than an independent agent) who habitually exercises an authority to conclude contracts, or regularly delivers goods or merchandise, or habitually secures orders in India, on behalf of the non-resident principal. In such a case, the profits of the non-resident or foreign company attributable to the business activities carried out in India become taxable under the Income-tax Act, 1961.

For the purposes of PE the agent must fill orders from a stock of goods or habitually exercise an authority to conclude contracts on behalf of or in the name of this foreign enterprise.

The question arises, how much profits could be said to be attributable to activities carried in India. Article 7 of the DTA provides the answer. It prescribes the rule whereby attributable profits are determined. For that matter the PE is assumed as an independent entity of the head office. The effect of article 7 is to limit the quantum of taxable income, which is arrived at by what is known as "attribution rule". Only so much profit is taxable in India as is attributable to the PE. The attributable profit is determined by apportionment of the total profits of the foreign company to its various parts if such apportionment is customary. Otherwise, it is done on the basis of a hypothesis that the profits which the PE might be expected to make were profits of a distinct and a separate enterprise engaged in the same or similar activities under the same and similar conditions and dealing wholly independently with the enterprise of which it is the PE (no profit is attributable by reason of mere purchase of goods or merchandise for the foreign company). All expenses incurred by the PE for the purpose of carrying on the activities are allowed as deduction, including executive and general expenses so incurred irrespective of where these are incurred.

Taxation of CAPTIVE BPO

nCA. GEETA DAS

This article elucidates upon the decision of the S upreme Court in Director of Income-tax v. Morgan Stanley & Co.’s case which settles many contentious issues in the field of international taxation, particularly with respect to the Business Process Outsourcing Unit of Multinational Corporations operating in India. This decision provides clear guidelines to the key issues, which bothered foreign investors. However, in the opinion of the author, certain points, which need clarification, have not been considered by the Court in proper perspective.

INTRODUCTION

1. On July 9, 2007, the Supreme Court of India pronounced its historic judgment in Director of Income-tax International Taxation v. Morgan Stanley & Co. [2007] 162 Taxman 165 that settles many contentious issues in the field of international taxation, particularly with respect to the captive Business Process Outsourcing Unit (BPO) of Multi-national Corporations (MNC) operating in India.

DECISION OF MORGAN STANLEY & CO.

2. The said decision is analyzed as under:

2.1. Factual Matrix - Morgan Stanley & Co. is an American based MNC in global banking and financial services. Its Indian arm, Morgan Stanley Advantages Services Pvt. Ltd (MSAS), functions as an outsourcing outfit engaged in activities including back office processing work in India (captive BPO). As this subsidiary has a fixed place of business for its operation, the tax administration considered a portion of the global income attributed to MSAS be taxed as Indian income as applicable to a service Permanent Establishment (PE).

Morgan Stanley & Co., however obtained a ruling from the Authority for Advance Ruling (AAR) regarding the taxation of MSAS that the captive BPO cannot be regarded as fixed place PE under article 5(1) of the DTAA, or agency PE under article 5(4). The AAR in the impugned ruling had also held that the service agreement between Morgan Stanley & Co. and MSAS dated April 14, 2005 would fall under the purview of article 5(2)(l ) and, consequently, tax would be levied on the net income of the Indian arm in accordance with the valuation procedure of the services rendered to the parent company as provided to an outsider under section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (‘the Act’).

Both the parties, the tax administration and Morgan Stanley & Co. appealed to the Supreme Court.

2.2. The relevant provisions and the Issues - Section 9 of the Act deals with business connections between a resident and a non-resident. In the provisions of section 90 of the Act, Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) overrides the domestic law and the assessee is taxed which is advantageous where such treaty exists. In accordance with the treaty between India and USA, business profit is taxable under article 7 of the DTAA provided such profits are attributed to PE as defined in article 5 of the DTAA.

The key issue, therefore, is whether the operation of MSAS constitutes PE for its back office operation in India under the existing provisions of the law.

The Finance Act, 2002 inserted the definition of PE vide section 92-F(iiia) which states, "The PE shall include a fixed place of business though which the business of the MNC is wholly or partly carried on." While the intent of this definition is in the inclusive sense to cover service PE, agency PE, construction PE, software PE, etc., the definition in the DTAA is in the exhaustive sense and article 5(3)(e) states, "notwithstanding the preceding provisions of the article {what is stated in article 5(1) or under article 5(2)}the term PE shall be deemed not to include maintenance of a fixed place of business solely for advertisement, scientific research or for activities which have a preparatory or auxiliary in character, for the enterprise."

2.3 The judgment : - The Supreme Court upheld the views of AAR that BPOs in India engaged in back office work of a parent company will not constitute PE under article 5(1).

As the BPO has no power to conclude any contract on behalf of the parent company, it does not give rise to agency PE under article 5(4). The Apex C ourt also agreed with the argument of Morgan Stanley & Co. that ‘stewardship’ activity of the parent company for maintaining the quality and confidentiality of work would not support applicability of article 5(2)(l) and, therefore, the BPO will not constitute a PE.

2.1 Arm’s length price payable to agent extinguishing assessment - The basis for this view is discussed as under : u In Circular (No. 23 of 1969) issued by the Central Board of Direct Taxes (‘CBDT’), it has been clarified that where a non-resident’s sales to Indian customers are secured through services of an agent in India, assessment in India of the income arising out of the transaction will be limited to the amount of profit which is attributable to the agent’s services. If the agents’ commission fully represents the value of the profit attributable to his service, it should prima facie extinguish the assessment.

The tax office had appealed to the Supreme Court of India on this issue, and a ruling is expected shortly.

On the other hand, where a foreign principal outsources the whole or part of its core revenue-generating business activities to an IT-enabled entity in India, such as the services of a travel agent, software developer, software maintenance, investment consultant, or debt collection service, and the IT-enabled entity in India renders the services either directly to the customers abroad, or through the non-resident principal, a considerable portion of the profits derived by the non-resident from its customers abroad, in the CBDT’s view, would be attributable to the activities performed by the IT-enabled entity in India.

However, the aforesaid Circular was withdrawn and another Circular No. 5 of 2004 was issued by the CBDT on the issue of taxability of IT enabled Business Process Outsourcing (‘BPO’) units which provided that the profits to be attributed to a PE in India have to be determined on the basis of the arm’s length principle and in accordance with the Indian transfer pricing regulations.

2.2 Something more than arm’s length price be taxed - As per OECD Discussion Draft on Attribution of Profits, 2004, India has taxing rights over two entities - the dependent agent enterprise (which may be a resident of the host country) and the dependent agent PE (which is a PE of a non-resident enterprise). Accordingly, attributation shall be achieved as follows :

u Differentiation between the assets used and risks assumed by the agent and the risks assumed by the principal with respect to the transactions as a whole;

u Profits associated with these assets and risks can be attributed to the PE (i.e., if the significant functions relevant to the assumption and/or management (subsequent to the transfer) of risks are performed by people in the PE and the significant functions relevant to the economic ownership of assets are performed by people in the PE)

u Profit to be determined by allocating an appropriate share of revenue from the transaction and deducting relevant costs (including head office allocation). Expenses include executive and general administrative expenses and these are deductible for calculating income of the PE. Similarly, consideration payable to agent shall be deductible. The expenses are deductible subject to any limitation under the domestic tax laws of India.

Approach of OECD

3. The approach of the OECD with regard to the attribution of profits to PE is based upon the following:

u A functional analysis which will result in the attribution of functions, assets and risks between the PE and its head office (HO) (It may be noted that risk should follow functions. Therefore, if functions are attributed to a PE, then the risks inherent in those functions are also attributable to the PE);

u Attribution of capital to the PE based on the assets and risks attributed to such PE;

u Recognition of transactions between the enterprise and third parties that are attributed to the PE and pricing of such transactions on an arm’s length basis;

u A recognition of dealings between the HO and the PE;

u A comparability analysis between dealings and uncontrolled transactions, established by applying analogically the Transfer Pricing Guidelines; and

Sub-clauses (c) and (d) address enhanced involvement of agent in the business of a non-resident, leading to increased tax base. They agree with the concept of Permanent Establishment ("PE") and taxation of business income under accepted international taxation principles as laid down in the Model tax conventions issued by the Organisation of Economic Co-operation and Development ("OECD") as well as the United Nations ("UN"). An interesting question that arises is whether the clarification provided here goes beyond the scope of the provisions in the ITA. Section 9 which extends the scope of taxation laid down under section 5 of the ITA, states that "all income accruing or arising, whether directly or indirectly, through or from any business connection in India6, or through or from any property in India, or through or from any asset or source of income in India, or through the transfer of a capital asset situate in India" would be deemed to accrue or arise in India. The most significant condition for extended scope of taxation is that there should be "business connection" in India. This term has not been defined in the ITA. However, it has been explained in various decisions by the Supreme Court of India. In the case of R. D. Aggarwal & Co.7 which was before Circular 23 was issued, the Apex Court held that there should be a real and intimate relation between trading activity carried on outside the taxable territories and trading activity carried on within the territories.

The ITA explains that if all the operations are not carried out in India then entire income will not be liable to taxation in India. Explanation 1( a) to section 9(1)(i) reads as follows :

"in the case of a business of which all the operations are not carried out in India, the income of the business deemed under this clause to accrue or arise in India shall be only such part of the income as is reasonably attributable to the operations carried out in India."

A combined reading of section 9(1)(i), the views expressed by the Supreme Court of India in the case of R. D. Aggarwal and the above Explanation, leads to the conclusion that the income of a non-resident will be liable to taxation in India only when the trading activity in India and the trading activity outside India, have real and intimate relationship. Further, only that income would be taxable in India which can be reasonably attributed to the operations carried out in India. In fact, the OECD subscribes to similar views.

OECD Model Tax Convention on PE and Transfer Pricing

It has been internationally accepted that the source country should not tax income of a foreign entity unless there is some longer economic relationship between the source country and the entity. This has been incorporated in the OECD Model tax treaty. Paragraph 1 of Article 7 of the Model states: "The profits of an enterprise of a Contracting State shall be taxable only in that State unless the enterprise carries on business in the other Contracting State through a permanent establishment situated therein. If the enterprise carries on business as aforesaid, the profits of the enterprise may be taxed in the other State but only so much of them as is attributable to that permanent establishment." When it comes to defining the term "permanent establishment" ("PE") Article 5 identifies the following categories – fixed PE, service PE and agency PE. So far as the first PE is concerned, broadly speaking, there is requirement of permanent relationship. Agency PE requires the agent to be dependent and some more conditions to be satisfied. Similarly, for service PE to exist, the services provided by a foreign entity should be over a sufficiently longer period and should satisfy certain conditions.

The authorized OECD approach on attribution of income to permanent establishments (July 2008) has led to an interplay between PE and the transfer pricing approaches. The authorized OECD approach rests on the foundation of Article 7(1) and Article 7(2) of the OECD Model Tax convention. As mentioned above, Article 7 (1) permits the host country to tax the "profits of the enterprise" but only so much as is "attributable to" a PE in the host country. Article 7(2) states that the profits to be attributed to the PE are the profits "it might be expected" to make if it were a distinct and separate enterprise dealing wholly independently with the enterprise of which it is a part.

Based on the above, the authorized OECD approach prescribes a two step approach for attributing profits to a PE. Step 1 is to hypothesize the PE as a "functionally separate entity" and Step 2 is to compute arm’s length remuneration as per the OECD transfer pricing guidelines.
