The year 2025 witnessed several landmark rulings in the field of direct taxation, with courts and tribunals addressing complex issues spanning permanent establishment, treaty abuse, capital gains, trusts, penalties, exemptions, and procedural law.

From the Supreme Court's reaffirmation of substance over form in cross-border arrangements to Tribunal decisions clarifying the scope of exemptions, rebates, and deeming provisions, these rulings have significantly influenced tax positions adopted by taxpayers and the Revenue alike.

This article presents a curated rewind of 25 key direct tax rulings delivered in 2025 that shaped legal interpretation, resolved long-standing controversies, and provided crucial guidance on the application of the Income-tax Act, international tax treaties, and allied laws.

1. 'Hyatt International' having pervasive control over the hotel's operations had fixed place PE in India: SC

Hyatt International Southwest Asia Ltd. v. Additional Director of Income-tax [2025] 176 taxmann.com 783 (SC)

Assessee-Hyatt International was engaged in rendering consultancy services in the hotel sector. It entered into two Strategic Oversight Services Agreements (SOSAs) with an Indian company regarding the hotels in Delhi and Mumbai. For the relevant assessment years, the Assessing Officer passed assessment orders taxing the hotel-related services rendered by the assessee on the ground that it has a Permanent Establishment (PE) in India in the form of a place of business under Article 5(1) of the DTAA.

The matter reached before the High Court. The High Court held that the assessee exercised pervasive and enforceable control over the hotel's strategic, operational, and financial dimensions. The High Court held that the assessee's role was not confined to high-level decision making but extended to substantive operational control and implementation.

The assessee's ability to enforce compliance, oversee operations, and derive profit-linked fees from the hotel's earnings demonstrates a clear and continuous commercial nexus and control with the hotel's core functions. This nexus satisfies the conditions necessary for the constitution of a Fixed Place PE under Article 5(1) of the India-UAE DTAA.

Aggrieved by the order, the assessee preferred an appeal to the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court held that the assessee exercised pervasive and enforceable control over the hotel's strategic, operational, and financial dimensions. Specifically, the agreement vested the assessee with powers to appoint and supervise the General Manager and other key personnel, implement human resource and procurement policies, control pricing, branding, and marketing strategies, manage operational bank accounts, and assign personnel to the hotel without requiring the owner's consent. These rights extend well beyond mere consultancy, indicating that the assessee was an active participant in the hotel's core operational activities.

The actual role of the assessee was not just advisory but extended to various other administrative roles. The 20-year duration of the SOSA, coupled with the assessee's continuous and functional presence, satisfied the tests of stability, productivity, and dependence. From the nature of functions carried out by the assessee, it cannot be said that they were performing merely "auxiliary" functions.

Rather, the functions performed by the assessee, through its staff operating from the hotel premises, were not just limited to setting up a pattern of activities for the hotel but were core and essential functions, clearly establishing their control over the day-to-day operations of the hotel. Therefore, the hotel premises clearly satisfy the criteria required to be classified as a "fixed place of business" or PE.

2. Supreme Court stays HC's ruling allowing tax relief to Tiger Global

Authority for Advance Rulings (Income-tax) v. Tiger Global International II Holdings [2025] 170 taxmann.com 706 (SC)

The Supreme Court has stayed the Delhi High Court ruling in the case of Tiger Global International II Holdings. The Apex Court held that issues raised by the Authority for Advance Rulings (Income-tax) in the petition require thorough consideration.

What was the Delhi High Court's ruling?

The Delhi High Court, in the case of Tiger Global International III Holdings [2024] 165 taxmann.com 850 (Delhi), overturned the Delhi Authority for Advance Ruling (AAR) decision that denied Tiger Global exemption on capital gains from the sale of its stake in Flipkart under the India-Mauritius Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA).

The High Court ruled that Tiger Global's transaction was legitimate and not aimed at tax avoidance, allowing it to claim tax benefits under the treaty's 'grandfathering clause' for capital gains on shares acquired before April 1, 2017. The court rejected the AAR's view that Tiger Global was merely a "see-through entity" controlled by a US-based individual.

Navigating the landscape of valuation for the imports

In the complex world of imports, businesses often consider the value of the physical goods to be paramount. However, they sometimes overlook that beyond the physical cargo lies something less visible yet crucial — the royalty/license fee payments. Royalties arise from licensing agreements which grant the importer rights inter alia to use manufacturing know-how, brand names, or software embedded within imported goods.

As the nature of contracts pertaining to imports/exports and associated license fee/royalty has evolved, the Customs valuation has also come a long way. Once upon a time, a physical shipment was all that customs authorities cared about for determining its value and imposition duties. Today's imports bundle licensed software, technology, trademarks, and other rights, making valuation of such shipments more complicated. While the goods themselves represent the tangible aspect for customs valuation, the accompanied intangible rights and their payments may significantly contribute to the overall value of the import transaction. This evolution sets the stage for courts to demystify when license fee/royalty should be included in the transaction value of the imported goods.

The recent judgement by CESTAT, New Delhi in the judgment of HCL Technologies Ltd. and SAP India Pvt. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Customs (Adjudication) [Final Order No. 51379-51462 of 2025 dated 29-9-2025] bring these complexities to the forefront. It deals with critical questions regarding includability of license fee in the value of the imported goods, specifically in the context of delivery of software through physical and electronic media.

Under the Lens: CESTAT's approach in the case of HCL Technologies Ltd.

Facts at a Glance

HCL Technologies Ltd. ('HCL') entered into an End-User License Agreement ('EULA') with SAP India Private Limited ('SAP India') to obtain non-exclusive and perpetual license to use propriety software, documentation and other information of SAP India. As per terms of the EULA, the software was to be delivered electronically. In the year 2006, SAP India raised substantial invoices on HCL for payment of license fee relating to rights provided under the EULA.

During the same time, HCL received some imported CDs containing SAP Software via courier, wherein a nominal value was declared under the courier bill of entry, for customs purposes. Perhaps, this is what caught the eye of the Customs Department – A CD with a software... only for pocket change?

An investigation was initiated against inter alia HCL for such imports. Upon conclusion of the investigation, the Customs Department rejected the declared value of the CDs under Rule 10A of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Price of Imported Goods) Rules, 1988 ('CVR') [now Rule 14 of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007] and sought to include the license fee in the valuation of imported CDs in terms of Rule 9(1)(c) of CVR.

The allegation of the Customs Department was that unless the license fee is paid, the software on the CD cannot be accessed or used; thereby, making the license fee integral to the transaction value of the imported CDs.

Tribunal's Verdict: Four Conditions for Royalty Inclusion in Customs Valuation

The Tribunal determined that for inclusion of royalties to the value of the imported goods, the following four key conditions under Rule 9(1)(c) of CVR needed to be satisfied:

1.

The license fee must relate to the imported goods;

2.

The fee must be payable directly or indirectly by the importer at the time of import;

3.

The license fee must be a condition of sale of the goods; and

4.

The fee must not already be included in the price actually paid or payable for the imported goods.

Guided by these conditions, the Tribunal took a closer look at the terms of the EULA entered between HCL&SAP India, and made the following findings:

The license fee was not related to the physical import of the CDs; rather, it was related to the intangible right to use the software in India. The EULA had itself provided electronic delivery as the mode of delivery of the software. Thus, the license fee was for usage of software rights and not for the import of physical CDs themselves.

The EULA provided for a trial period which allowed HCL limited software access without payment of license fee. The obligation for full payment, per the terms of EULA, would only be triggered only if HCL opted for full license post this trial. Therefore, HCL was not required to pay the license fee at the time of import.

2. Certain issues arose for consideration of AAR. These are answered as under :

(i)Whether, on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, Morgan Stanley & Co. Incorporated (‘the applicant’) would be regarded as having a Permanent Establishment (‘PE’) in India under the provisions of article 5 of the Agreement for Avoidance of Double Taxation and Prevention of Fiscal Evasion with respect to taxes on income and capital gains entered into between the Government of the Republic of India and the Government of the United States of America (‘the Treaty’), and specifically :

(a)Whether the applicant (parent company) would be regarded as having a PE in India under article 5 of the Treaty on account of the services rendered by Morgan Stanley Advantage Services (P.) Ltd. (MSAS) under the Draft Services Agreement proposed to be entered into by it with the applicant (‘Agreement’)?

Ans. MSAS (the Indian subsidiary) is not the PE of the applicant in India under the provisions of article 5(1) of the Treaty. This is because the primary condition of the business of the parent company having been carried on wholly or partly by the Indian subsidiary is not getting satisfied. In other words, the Indian subsidiary has only performed back-office work and not any revenue generation activities for the parent company. Hence, both paragraphs (1) and (2) of article 5 need to be satisfied to hold presence of a PE.

(b)Whether MSAS would be regarded as constituting an agency PE of the applicant under article 5(4)?

Ans. MSAS would not constitute an agency PE of the applicant under article 5(4);

(c)Whether the applicant would be regarded as having a PE in India under article 5(2)(l) if it were to send some of its employees to India for undertaking certain stewardship activities as described in paragraph 3 in Annexure II ?

Ans. Once the employees are sent by the applicant on deputation for stewardship activities, they would be actively involved in the key managerial activities of MSAS as has been pointed out above. It follows that the ingredients of paragraph (2)(l) of article 5 are satisfied and, therefore, MSAS would constitute the PE of the applicant/Morgan group. More specifically it held that MSAS would be regarded as the PE of the applicant in India under article 5(2)(l) of the Treaty if it were to send some of its employees to India for undertaking stewardship activities as described in paragraph 3 in Annexure II for a period beyond ninety days ;

(d)Whether the applicant would be regarded as having a PE in India under article 5(2)(l) of the Treaty if it were to send some of its employees to India on deputation in the employment of MSAS ?

Ans. MSAS would be regarded as the PE of the applicant in India under article 5(2)(l) of the Treaty if it were to send some of its employees to India on deputation in the employment of MSAS for a period beyond ninety days ;

(ii)Whether, on the facts and in the circumstances of the case and in the light of the provisions of section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (‘the Act’) read with rules 10B and 10C of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 (‘the Rules’), the Transactional Net Margin Method (‘TNMM’) is the most appropriate method for the determination of the arm’s length price in respect of transactions between the applicant and MSAS ?

Ans. The question is liable to be rejected in view of the first proviso to sub-section (2) of section 245R of the Act ;

(iii)Whether, on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, a mark-up of 29 per cent (using the TNMM for the bench marking analysis) on the operating costs incurred by MSAS for providing services to the applicant would meet the arm’s length test as prescribed under Chapter X of the Act ?

Ans. Not answered since dropped.

Section 9(6)(b) defines 'royalty' to include consideration for the use or right to use any industrial, commercial or scientific equipment. The classification of data centre services as 'royalty' has been a subject of judicial scrutiny. Indian courts, such as the Mumbai ITAT in Rackspace US, Inc. v. DCIT [2021] 124 taxmann.com 92, have held that income from cloud hosting and ancillary services was neither royalty nor Fees for Technical Services (FTS). The Tribunal observed that the agreement was for providing hosting services simpliciter, not for the use or leasing of equipment, as customers did not have physical control or possession over the servers. If the foreign company retains control and operational responsibility for the data centre infrastructure and merely provides a service to overseas users, the income is unlikely to be classified as royalty. Furthermore, in case the users are overseas, the requirement that the royalty be for the use of a right/property in a business/income source in India would generally not be met.

The use of a data centre by a foreign company providing services to overseas or Indian users may not give rise to royalty income under a DTAA, given the specific interpretation of 'royalty' in these treaties and consistent judicial precedents. The definition of 'royalty' in most DTAAs entered into by India is typically narrower than the broad definition provided under section 9(6)(b) of the ITA 2025. DTAAs often require a more direct nexus to the use or right to use specific intellectual property or equipment, or the transfer of technical know-how. For payments to be classified as royalty for the 'use or right to use industrial, commercial or scientific equipment' under a DTAA, judicial pronouncements39 consistently emphasise that the payer (user) must have physical control or possession over the equipment.

Therefore, if the data centre services involve providing access to software, platforms, or infrastructure without transferring the underlying intellectual property rights or granting users control over or possession of the equipment, the income is unlikely to be characterised as royalty under the DTAA. It would typically be considered business profits, taxable only if a Permanent Establishment (PE) exists in India.

3.4-4 'Transfer of all or any rights' v. 'Transfer or grant of all or any rights' [Section 9(6)(b) & 9(6)(c)(i) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Explanations 2 & 4 to Section 9(1)(vi) of the ITA 1961)] Explanation 2 to Section 9(1)(vi) defines the meaning of 'royalty' which includes "the transfer of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence) in respect of a patent, invention, model, design, secret formula or process or trade mark or similar property", and Explanation 4 to section 9(1)(vi) clarified that the transfer of any right, property or information shall include transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software (including granting of a licence) irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred.

Under the ITA 1961, the phrase "the transfer of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence)…" was used in Explanation 2(i) & 2(v) to section 9(1)(vi), whereas the phrase "the transfer of all or any rights" was used in Explanation 4 to section 9(1)(vi). However, under the ITA 2025, the former phrase has been replaced with the new phrase "the transfer or grant of all or any rights (including the granting of a licence)…", and the latter phrase has been replaced with the new phrase "the transfer or grant of all or any rights". The corresponding provisions under the ITA 2025 are sub-clauses (i) and (vi) of section 9(6)(b) and sub-clause (i) of section 9(6)(c), respectively.

This explicit insertion of 'or grant' attempts to cover any form of allowing the use of rights, whether it is a full transfer (alienation of ownership) or a mere permission to use (grant). This appears to be an attempt to nullify the Supreme Court's ruling in Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 42 (SC). By explicitly including 'grant', the legislature intends to emphasise that payments for the use of software, patents, copyrights, and other intellectual properties, even if they do not involve a full 'transfer' of copyright or a 'parting with an interest' in the underlying rights, are brought within the ambit of royalty. The intent is to tax payments for the mere 'use' or 'right to use' such properties as royalty, irrespective of whether the transaction constitutes an outright sale of the underlying intellectual property or a mere licence. However, for non-residents, the tax implications of this expanded definition of royalty must always be considered in light of any applicable DTAAs that India has with other countries. While the ITA 2025 aims to broaden the domestic definition, it does not automatically override the DTAA provisions. The Supreme Court's ruling in Engineering Analysis was largely based on the DTAA provisions, and the amendment to Section 9(1)(vi) might not change the interpretation of DTAA articles if the DTAA's definition of royalty is narrower.

Note: Although this provision was not amended by the Finance Act, 2026, the above discussion highlights the changes introduced in the ITA 2025 compared to the ITA 1961.

3.5 The cap on the investment by an eligible investment fund has been increased from 20% to 25% [Section 9 and Schedule I of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 9A of the ITA 1961 Act)]

Section 9A of the ITA 1961 provides a special regime for offshore funds. It provides that in the case of an eligible investment fund, the fund management activity carried out through an eligible fund manager acting on behalf of such fund shall not constitute a business connection in India of the said fund. Further, an eligible investment fund shall not be deemed resident in India merely because the eligible fund manager undertaking fund management activities on its behalf is located in India. Thus, this exemption from the general rules for the determination of business connection and 'resident status' of offshore funds and fund management activity undertaken on their behalf is allowed on fulfilment of the conditions explained below:

(a)

The offshore fund should be an eligible investment fund.

(b)

The fund management activity of such a fund should be managed by an eligible fund manager.

The eligible investment fund means a fund established or incorporated, or registered outside India, which collects funds from its members for investing it for their benefit and fulfils the prescribed conditions. One such prescribed condition under the ITA 1961 is that the fund's investment in any entity does not exceed 20% of the fund's corpus, and that the fund does not make any investment in its associate entity.

Under the ITA 2025, this maximum capping on investment in any entity has been increased from 20% to 25%, and all other conditions remain the same.

Most DTAAs between India and other countries define 'royalties' to include payments for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial, or scientific equipment. If the specific DTAA between India and the country of which the foreign country is a resident includes 'payments for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment' in its definition of royalty, then the income would be classified as royalty under the DTAA. In such a case, the income would be taxable in India at the rate specified in the DTAA, provided the foreign company is the beneficial owner and the income is not effectively connected to a PE in India. If the DTAA does not include such payments in its royalty definition (under the OECD Model), the income would be treated as business profits and taxable in India only if the foreign company has a PE in India and the profits are attributable to that PE.

8.5-11d Classification as FTS - Section 9(7)(a) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 9(1)(vii) of the ITA 1961) deems income by way of fees for technical services (FTS) to accrue or arise in India. Section 9(7)(b) defines 'fees for technical services' as any consideration for the rendering of any managerial, technical or consultancy services (including the provision of services of technical or other personnel). Where the foreign company also provides the installation and training services for the capital goods, equipment, or tooling to the Indian manufacturer to use them, any fees paid by the Indian manufacturer for these services would squarely fall within the definition of FTS under section 9(7)(b). The income is deemed to accrue or arise in India as it is payable by a resident of India.

Most DTAAs have a specific article on FTS (Fees for Included Services). These articles may include a 'make available' clause, meaning the services must not only be technical but also 'make available' technical knowledge, experience, skill, know-how, or processes to the recipient. If the foreign company is merely providing equipment and not imparting any technical knowledge or skills to the Indian manufacturer that enable the latter to apply the technology independently, the 'make available' test (if present in the DTAA) would not be met. In such a situation, the FTS will not be taxable in India. If the DTAA does not explicitly contain a 'make available' clause, then any service of a managerial, technical, or consultancy nature will be taxable as FTS.

(a)

Whether the foreign company has a PE in India

(b)

Whether the income is such that the presumptive scheme as specified in Section 61: Table Sl. No. 6 applies (corresponding to Section 44BBD of the ITA 1961) (Business of providing services or technology in India, for the purposes of setting up an electronics manufacturing facility).

The taxable income, taking these factors into account, will be as follows.

Business income connected to PE in India

If the foreign company has a PE in India, and the business income earned in India is connected to such PE, the tax liability in such a case shall be computed as per the ITA. If the conditions of section 61: Table Sl. No. 6 is fulfilled; the taxable business income shall be computed on a presumptive basis at the rate of 25% of the specified amount. If conditions are not fulfilled, the actual business income shall be computed as per the general provisions.

Business income not connected to PE in India

If the non-resident does not have a PE in India, the business income earned by him in India shall not be taxable in India. In such a situation, the presumptive scheme of section 61: Table Sl. No. 6 will have no relevance.

In such a scenario, business profits are not taxable in India as there is no PE in India. 2.8-9b Scope of income under ITA v. DTAA - Under domestic law, fees for technical services are taxable under section 9(1)(vii) of the ITA, which provides a detailed definition of the term. However, under the DTAA, such income is taxable under Article 12, which provides a narrow definition.

The judicial fora in India, including the Hon'ble SC, have often held that the provisions of the DTAA prevail over the provisions of the ITA when determining whether a particular income is covered under the definition of 'fees for technical services'.

For example, in treaties entered into by India with some countries, viz. Canada, Netherlands, Portugal, UK, USA, etc., the term fees for technical services do not include 'managerial service' though the same is included in the provisions of domestic law.

Further, in DTAAs entered into by India with some countries, such as Canada, the Netherlands, Portugal, Singapore, the UK, the USA, etc., services provided by the assessee are treated as fees for technical services only if they satisfy the 'make available' test.

In the above situations, the judicial fora have held that, though the services are covered under the definition of 'fees for technical services' under domestic law, as such services are not covered under the DTAA, payment made for services are not taxable in the source country. This is because the provisions of DTAA override the provisions of domestic law.

Similarly, section 9(1) (vi) of the ITA deals with the definition of royalty, and the scope of royalty is much wider than the definition in Article 12 of the DTAA. Applying the same ratio, the taxpayer may not be taxed in India as the transaction entered by the taxpayer may not fall under the definition of royalty under the DTAA, though the same is treated as royalty under section 9(1)(vi) of the ITA.

2.8-9c Computation of income under ITA v. DTAA - The computation of income from providing services or technology, as mentioned in section 44BBD, depends on two factors - the nature of income and the existence of PE in India.

(a)

Where the nature is business income, and the non-resident has a PE in India, the income shall be computed as per section 44BBD.

(b)

Where the nature is business income but the non-resident does not have a PE in India, the income shall not be taxable in India in view of Article 7 (Business Profits) of the relevant DTAA.

(c)

Where the nature is royalty or FTS, and the non-resident has a PE in India, the income shall be computed as per section 44BBD [see Para 2.7-1].

(d)

Where the nature is royalty or FTS but the non-resident does not have a PE in India, the income shall be computed as per section 44BBD.

2.8-9d Rate of tax under ITA v. DTAA - The tax rate to be applied to the income computed under section 44BBD shall depend upon two factors - nature of income, such as royalty, FTS or other business income, and whether connected to PE in India.

(a)

Where the nature is business income, and the non-resident has a PE in India, the income computed as per section 44BBD shall be taxable at the applicable rate.

(b)

Where the nature is business income but the non-resident does not have a PE in India, the income shall not be taxable in India in view of Article 7 (Business Profits) of the relevant DTAA.

(c)

Where the nature of income is royalty or FTS, and the non-resident has a PE in India, the income computed as per section 44BBD shall be taxable at the applicable rate.

(d)

Where the nature of the income is royalty or FTS but the non-resident does not have a PE in India, the income computed as per section 44BBD shall be taxable at the applicable rate.

In view of the proviso to section 44BBD(2) which excludes the applicability of section 115A, the concessional tax rate for the royalty and FTS specified under section 115A shall not be available if the presumptive income from the royalty or FTS is computed under section 44BBD.

2.8-9e Levy of surcharge under ITA v. DTAA - As per the provisions of ITA, income tax payable by the taxpayer shall be increased by applicable surcharge and cess. On the other hand, Article 12 of most DTAAs state that FTS earned in India are taxable at the rate of 10%.

The corresponding provisions under the ITA 2025 are sub-clauses (i) and (vi) of section 9(6)(b) and sub-clause (i) of section 9(6)(c), respectively. This explicit insertion of 'or grant' attempts to cover any form of allowing the use of rights, whether it is a full transfer (alienation of ownership) or a mere permission to use (grant). This appears to be an attempt to nullify the Supreme Court's ruling in Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 42 (SC). By explicitly including 'grant', the legislature intends to emphasise that payments for the use of software, patents, copyrights, and other intellectual properties, even if they do not involve a full 'transfer' of copyright or a 'parting with an interest' in the underlying rights, are brought within the ambit of royalty. The intent is to tax payments for the mere 'use' or 'right to use' such properties as royalty, irrespective of whether the transaction constitutes an outright sale of the underlying intellectual property or a mere licence. However, for non-residents, the tax implications of this expanded definition of royalty must always be considered in light of any applicable DTAAs that India has with other countries. While the ITA 2025 aims to broaden the domestic definition, it does not automatically override the DTAA provisions. The Supreme Court's ruling in Engineering Analysis was largely based on the DTAA provisions, and the amendment to Section 9(1)(vi) might not change the interpretation of DTAA articles if the DTAA's definition of royalty is narrower.

Note: Although this provision was not amended by the Finance Act, 2026, the above discussion highlights the changes introduced in the ITA 2025 compared to the ITA 1961.

3.5 The cap on the investment by an eligible investment fund has been increased from 20% to 25% [Section 9 and Schedule I of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 9A of the ITA 1961 Act)]

Section 9A of the ITA 1961 provides a special regime for offshore funds. It provides that in the case of an eligible investment fund, the fund management activity carried out through an eligible fund manager acting on behalf of such fund shall not constitute a business connection in India of the said fund. Further, an eligible investment fund shall not be deemed resident in India merely because the eligible fund manager undertaking fund management activities on its behalf is located in India. Thus, this exemption from the general rules for the determination of business connection and 'resident status' of offshore funds and fund management activity undertaken on their behalf is allowed on fulfilment of the conditions explained below:

(a)

The offshore fund should be an eligible investment fund.

(b)

The fund management activity of such a fund should be managed by an eligible fund manager.

The eligible investment fund means a fund established or incorporated, or registered outside India, which collects funds from its members for investing it for their benefit and fulfils the prescribed conditions. One such prescribed condition under the ITA 1961 is that the fund's investment in any entity does not exceed 20% of the fund's corpus, and that the fund does not make any investment in its associate entity.

Under the ITA 2025, this maximum capping on investment in any entity has been increased from 20% to 25%, and all other conditions remain the same.

Note: Although this provision was not amended by the Finance Act, 2026, the above discussion highlights the changes introduced in the ITA 2025 compared to the ITA 1961.

Payment can be made as a consideration for the use or right to use of the defined property only when such property is in existence at the time of use. 2.2-1a-2 MEANING OF TERM 'SOURCE' - The term 'source' has been explained by the Supreme Court as follows: "Source in relation to an income has been construed to be where the transaction of sale takes place and not where the item of value, which was the subject of the transaction, was acquired or derived from. HTIL and Vodafone are offshore companies and since the sale took place outside India, applying the source test, the source is also outside India, unless legislation ropes in such transactions." [Vodafone International Holdings B. V. v. UOI [2012] 6 SCC 6131]

Thus, source is where the transaction of sale has taken place. If the specified activity has taken place outside India, it may be argued that the source is not in India within the meaning of section 9(1)(i).

In CIT v. Havells India Ltd. [2012] 21 taxmann.com 476/208 Taxman 114 (Delhi), the Court had to interpret section 9(1)(vii)(b) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 which provides that fees for technical services do not accrue or arise in India to the extent they are paid by a resident for utilizing the services for making or earning any income from any "source" outside India. It observed as follows:

"Section 9(1)(vii)(b) contemplates a source located outside India. It is difficult to conceptualise the place/situs of the person who make payment for the export sales as the source located outside India from which assessee earned profits. The export contracts obviously are concluded in India and the assessee's products are sent outside India under such contracts. The manufacturing activity is located in India. The source of income is created at the moment when the export contracts are concluded in India. Thereafter the goods are exported in pursuance of the contract and the export proceeds are sent by the importer and are received in India. The importer of the assessee's products is no doubt situated outside India, but he cannot be regarded as a source of income. The receipt of the sale proceeds emanate from him from outside India. He is, therefore, only the source of the monies received. The income component of the monies or the export receipts is located or situated only in India. We are making a distinction between the source of the income and the source of the receipt of the monies. In order to fall within the second exception provided in Section 9(1)(vii)(b) of the Act, the source of the income, and not the receipt, should be situated outside India. That condition is not satisfied in the present case."

Thus, the Court held that export sales proceeds received from goods manufactured and exported from India do not constitute a "source" outside India but is a source in India. Similarly, for the non-resident who sells the goods from outside India, it could be argued that it constitutes a source in the country from which the sale is made and not in India where the customer is situated.

"As far as royalty on export sales is concerned, that amount is also exempt under section 9(1)(vi). Since the source for royalty is from the source situate outside India, the royalty paid on export sales is not taxable."

Similarly it could be argued that the source for sale from outside India is not in India.

(i) the transfer of all or any rights in respect of any right, property or information includes and has always included transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software (including granting of a licence) irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred (Explanation 4).

(ii) royalty includes and has always included consideration in respect of any right, property or information, whether or not (a) the possession or control of such right, property or information is with the payer; (b) such right, property or information is used directly by the payer; (c) the location of such right, property or information is in India (Explanation 5).

(iii) the expression 'process' includes and shall be deemed to have always included transmission by satellite (including up-linking, amplification, conversion for down-linking of any signal), cable, optic fibre or by any other similar technology, whether or not such process is secret (Explanation 6).

2.8.2 Object

The objective of the amendments as explained in the Memorandum explaining the provisions of Finance Bill, 2012 is as follows:

"II. Section 9(1)(vi) provides that any income payable by way of royalty in respect of any right, property or information is deemed to be accruing or arising in India. The term "royalty" has been defined in Explanation 2 which means consideration received or receivable for transfer of all or any right in respect of certain rights, property or information. Some judicial decisions have interpreted this definition in a manner which has raised doubts as to whether consideration for use of computer software is royalty or not; whether the right, property or information has to be used directly by the payer or is to be located in India or control or possession of it has to be with the payer. Similarly, doubts have been raised regarding the meaning of the term processed.

Considering the conflicting decisions of various courts in respect of income in nature of royalty and to restate the legislative intent, it is further proposed to amend the Income-tax Act in following manner:-

(i) To amend section 9(1)(vi) to clarify that the consideration for use or right to use of computer software is royalty by clarifying that transfer of all or any rights in respect of any right, property or information as mentioned in Explanation 2, includes and has always included transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software (including granting of a licence) irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred.

(ii) To amend section 9(1)(vi) to clarify that royalty includes and has always included consideration in respect of any right, property or information, whether or not

(a) the possession or control of such right, property or information is with the payer;

(b) such right, property or information is used directly by the payer;

(c) the location of such right, property or information is in India.

(iii) To amend section 9(1)(vi) to clarify that the term "process" includes and shall be deemed to have always included transmission by satellite (including up-linking, amplification, conversion for down-linking of any signal), cable, optic fibre or by any other similar technology, whether or not such process is secret.

These amendments will take effect retrospectively from 1st June, 1976 and will accordingly apply in relation to the assessment year 1977-78 and subsequent assessment years."

2.8.3 Analysis

2.8.3.1 Computer software (Explanation 4)

2.8.3.1.1 Paraphrasing the Explanation 4, it now provides that transfer of all or any rights in respect of any right, property or information includes and has always included :

♦ transfer of all right for use (of1) a computer software

♦ transfer of any right for use (of1) a computer software

♦ right to use a computer software

♦ grant of license to use a computer software.

For the above purpose the medium through which the aforesaid right is transferred is irrelevant.

2.8.3.1.2 Explanation 2(v) to section 9(1)(vi) provides that royalty includes consideration for the transfer of all or any rights (including the granting of a license) in respect of any copyright.

There has been a huge controversy as to whether consideration for sale/supply of software is covered by the expression royalty or not. To illustrate, in the following cases, it was held that the consideration was not royalty :

♦ DIT v. Ericsson AB [2012] 204 Taxman 192/[2011] 16 taxmann.com 371 (Delhi)

Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. [2011] 16 taxmann.com 141/203 Taxman 477 (Kar.); CIT v. Synopsis International Old Ltd. [2012] 28 taxmann.com 162/[2013] 212 Taxman 454 (Kar.)] and review petition dismissed in Commissioner of Income-tax v. GE India Technology Centre (P.) Ltd. [2024] 161 taxmann.com 707/469 ITR 389 (SC)]. Telecasting rights - Where payment made by assessee, a Singapore based company, to GCC (also tax resident of Singapore) for acquiring cricket telecast rights throughout licence territory including India had no connection with marketing activities carried out through its alleged PE in India, such payment held not to be 'royalty' and, hence, not chargeable to tax in India [DIT v. Set Satellite (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. [2014] 45 taxmann.com 100/225 Taxman 1 (Bom.)].

Telecom services outside India - Assessee, engaged in business of providing telecom services to its subscribers in India, entered into agreements with non-resident telecom operators for providing bandwidth and interconnect capacity outside India, in such a case payment made in consideration of said services held to be in the nature of 'royalty' [DDIT v. Vodafone South Ltd. [2014] 45 taxmann.com 227 (Kar.)].

Bandwidth payments made by Indian customers to a Singapore-based company for International Private Leased Circuit (IPLC) for providing end-to-end internet connectivity outside India (where connectivity for Indian leg was provided by VSNL due to Indian regulatory requirement) was taxable as 'royalty' [Verizon Communications Singapore Pte. Ltd. v. ITO [2013] 39 taxmann.com 70/[2014] 224 Taxman 237 (Mag.) (Mad.)].

Where assessee-company, a tax resident of Singapore, was providing bandwidth services to various Indian telecom operators and services were provided from outside India, since there was neither a right to use process nor there was a transfer of technology consideration received by assessee for providing such services was not taxable as 'royalty' under section 9(1)(vi) [Commissioner of Income-tax (International Taxation) v. Telstra Singapore Pte. Ltd. [2024] 165 taxmann.com 85 (Delhi)/[2024] 467 ITR 302 (Delhi)].

User manual - Where contract for supply of equipment and spare parts included stipulations for giving information so as to guide Indian party to install equipment at site and thereafter to use it, payment to Danish company held not to be 'royalty' since payment was made towards supply of equipments on principal-to-principal basis [DIT v. Haldor Topsoe [2014] 48 taxmann.com 67/225 Taxman 105 (Bom.)].

Other illustrations held not constitute 'royalty' - (1) Sum received for permitting the use of certain marks and intellectual property belonging to the assessee (a UK based company) for privilege of hosting and staging Formula F1 championship race which had been strictly confined and limited to use only for the promotion of the event and for no other purpose held not to be 'royalty' but 'business income' [Formula One World Championship Ltd. v. CIT [2017] 80 taxmann.com 347/248 Taxman 192 (SC)].

(2) Where assessee-company developed basic engine and sent the same to a non-resident company of Austria to design a new 3-valve cylinder head for improvement of fuel efficiency, performance and meeting Indian emission standard, payment made to Austrian company would not constitute 'royalty' [DIT v. TVS Motors Co. Ltd. [2018] 99 taxmann.com 40/259 Taxman 140 (Mad.)].

(3) Where subscription charges were received by TV channel operator from customers enabling them to view channels, since said receipt was not for transfer of any copyright in literary, artistic or scientific work, it could not be categorized as 'royalty income' [CIT v. MSM Satellite (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. [2019] 106 taxmann.com 353/265 Taxman 376 (Bom.)]. Also see, CIT v. Springer Nature Customer Services Centre GMBH [2023] 152 taxmann.com 277/294 Taxman 167 (Delhi).

(4) Amount received by assessee for licence of its product, which was embedded software, was not royalty, rather it was business income [CIT v. Bently Nevada LLC [2020] 114 taxmann.com 101 (Delhi), SLP granted inCIT v. Bently Nevada LLC [2020] 114 taxmann.com 102/270 Taxman 95 (SC)].

6.7 Section 80HHE provides for deduction in respect of profits and gains from software exports. As a measure to provide benefit to a supporting software developer exporting software through others, a new proviso to section 80HHE(1) has been inserted with effect from assessment year 1999-2000. The said proviso provides that where an assessee, being an exporting company engaged in the export out of India of computer software, issues a certificate in a prescribed form, that in respect of the amount of the export specified therein, the deduction under section 80HHE(1) is to be allowed to a supporting software developer, than the amount of deduction available to the assessee shall be reduced by such an amount which bears to the total profits derived by the assessee from the export, the same proportion as the amount of the export turnover specified in such certificate bears to the total export turnover of the assessee.

For this purpose,—

(i) exporting company has been defined as a company making actual export of computer software.

(ii) supporting software developer has been defined as an Indian company or a person (other than a company) resident in India developing and selling computer software to an exporting company for the purpose of export.

Further, a new sub-section (1A) has been inserted to provide that where the supporting software developer has developed and sold computer software to an exporting company in respect of which the said company has issued a certificate in the prescribed form in accordance with the provisions of section 80HHE(1) read with the proviso, a deduction will be allowed in computing the total income of the assessee to the extent of the profits derived by the assessee from the developing and selling of computer software to the exporting company in respect of which the certificate has been issued by the said company.

For the purposes of computing the profits derived by the supporting software developer as referred to in sub-section (1A), a new section 80HHE(3A) has been inserted which provides that

(i) where the business carried on by the supporting software developer consists exclusively of developing and selling of computer software to one or more exporting companies solely engaged in exports, the whole of the profits of such business shall be deemed as profits derived by the assessee;

(ii) where the business carried on by a supporting software developer does not consist exclusively of developing and selling of computer software to one or more exporting companies, the profit derived by the supporting software developer from sale of such software shall be the amount which bears to the profits of the business the same proportion as the turnover in respect of sale to the respective exporting company bears to the total turnover of the business carried on by the assessee.

The new sub-section (4A) provides that the deduction to the supporting software developer shall not be admissible unless he furnishes in the prescribed form along with his return of income -

(i) the report of an accountant, as defined in the Explanation below sub-section (2) of section 288, certifying that the deduction has been correctly claimed on the basis of the profits of the supporting software developer in respect of sale of computer software export to the exporting company; and

(ii) a certificate from the exporting company containing such particulars as may be prescribed and verified in the manner prescribed that in respect of the export turnover mentioned in the certificate, the exporting company has not claimed deduction under this section. The certificate issued by the exporting company shall be duly certified by the auditor auditing the accounts of the exporting assessee under the provisions of the Act or under any other law.

6.7-1 Amendment in definition of computer software for the purposes of section 80HHE - The definition of computer software has been amended to include any customised electronic data which is transmitted from India to any place outside India by any means.

such non-resident carries on business in India through a permanent establishment or performs professional services from a fixed place of profession in India; and

2.4-3 Treaties -Most of the treaties entered into by India provide in Article 7.3 that the computation of profits of a Permanent Establishment shall be done 'in accordance with the provisions of and subject to the limitations of' the local law. In Ericsson Telephone Corporation India AB v. CIT [1997] 224 ITR 203 and Advance Ruling P. No. 13 of 1995, In re, the Authority of Advance Rulings held that in view of the word 'subject to the limitation of local law', Article 7.3 is governed by section 44D of the Act and if no deduction is allowable pursuant to section 44D, the assessee is subject to gross basis of taxation, even under Article 7.3. Doubts have been raised about the correctness of the rulings.

If they do not lay down the correct law, the position would be as follows :

Provisions of section 44DA will govern the computation of profits of a Permanent Establishment in cases where the conditions mentioned in the section are fulfilled.

In all other cases, a view could be taken that the assessee will be governed under Article 7.3 by net basis of taxation on general principles.

2.4-4 Meaning of the term 'effectively connected' -The term 'effectively connected' is used in Article 12.3 of the OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital (January 2003) and Article 12.4 of the UN Model Convention. Accordingly, it is used in many treaties entered into by India. At the same time, it is not used elsewhere in the Act. In the circumstances, it appears that the interpretation of this term under the Treaties should generally be applicable for interpreting this term under the Act.

2.4-5 Transfer Pricing -The provisions of transfer pricing under sections 92 to 92F of the Act will also be applicable.

2.4-6 Audit Report -Section 44DA provides that the assessee shall get his accounts audited by an accountant and furnish along with the return of income, the report of such audit in prescribed form. Curiously, unlike sections 44BB and 44BBB, it does not state that the audit report should be as required under section 44AB of the Act. It appears that this is an inadvertent lapse and the position will be clarified by the Central Board of Direct Taxes or by appropriate legislative changes.

2.4-7 Deduction of tax at source -These sections are applicable to non-residents having income from royalties or fees for technical services. Section 195(1) of the Act provides that any person responsible for making payment to a non-resident in respect of any sum chargeable under the provisions of the Act shall deduct tax at source at the rates in force. For deduction of tax at lower or nil rate in respect of payments covered by the amended section, the payees will have to obtain certificates from the assessing officer under section 195(3) or 197(1) or the payer will have to obtain a certificate from the assessing officer under section 195(2).

The amendment provides that 'royalty' shall not include amounts referred to in section 44BB. Section 44BB, inter alia, provides that in the case of a non-resident assessee engaged in the business of supply of plant and machinery on hire, used or to be used in the exploration for and exploitation of mineral oils, 10% of the aggregate of the amounts which have been specified in the section shall be deemed to be profits and gains of the business. Thus, hire charges for the plant and machinery used for exploration, etc., of mineral oils shall not be treated as 'royalty' and shall continue to be taxed under section 44BB.

The amendment to section 9 brings it in line with the Double Tax Conventions (DTCs) entered into by India which provide that 'royalty' includes consideration for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment. It may be noted, however, that the definition of 'royalties' in Article 12(2) of OECD Model was amended in 1992 by excluding payments for the use, or right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment.

[1991] 190 ITR 626, the Calcutta High Court has held that where there is an outright sale or purchase, the consideration is for the transfer of designs, secret formula, etc., and cannot be treated as royalty. Issues relating to export of computer software - Note the following issues —

The Indian Software Industry has been the beneficiary of direct tax incentives under the provisions like sections 10A, 10AA & 10B of the Income-tax Act, 1961 in respect of their profits derived from the export of computer software. These provisions prescribe incentives to "units" or "undertakings", established under different schemes, which are/were deriving profits from export of computer software subject to fulfilling the prescribed conditions.

2. It has been represented by the software companies that several issues arising from the above mentioned provisions are giving rise to disputes between them and the Income-tax authorities leading to denial of tax benefits and consequent litigation and, therefore, require clarification. Various issues highlighted by the Software Industry have been examined by the Board and the following clarifications are hereby issued -

(i) (a) Whether "On-Site" development of Computer Software Qualifies as an export activity for tax benefits under sections 10A, 10AA and 10B of the Income-tax Act, 1961; and

(b) Whether receipts from deputation of Technical Manpower for such "On-Site" Software development abroad at the Client's place are eligible for deduction under sections 10A, 10AA and 10B.

(a)

CBDT had earlier issued a Circular (Circular No. 694, dated 23-11-1994) which provided that a unit should not be denied tax-holiday under section 10A or 10B on the ground that the computer software was prepared 'on-site', as long as it was a product of the unit, i.e., it is produced by the Unit. However, certain doubts appear to have arisen following the insertion of Explanation 3 to sections 10A and 10B (vide Finance Act, 2001) and Explanation 2 to section 10AA (vide Special Economic Zones Act, 2005) providing that "the profits and gains derived from on site development of computer software (including services for development of software) outside India shall be deemed to be the profits and gains derived from the export of computer software outside India", and a clarification has been sought on the impact of the Explanation on the tax-benefits as compared to the situation that existed prior to the amendments.

The matter has been examined. In view of the position of law as it stands now, it is clarified that the software developed abroad at a client's place would be eligible for benefits under the respective provisions, because these would amount to 'deemed export' and tax benefits would not be denied merely on this ground. However, since the benefits under these provisions can be availed of only by the units or undertakings set up under specified schemes in India, it is necessary that there must exist a direct and intimate nexus or connection of development of software done abroad with the eligible units set up in India and such development of software should be pursuant to a contract between the client and the eligible unit. To this extent, Circular No. 694, dated 23-11-1994 stands further clarified.

(b)

It has also been brought to notice that it is a common practice in the software industry to depute Technical Manpower abroad (at the client's place) for software development activities (like upgradation, testing, maintenance, modification, trouble-shooting etc.), which often require frequent interaction with the clients located outside India. Due to the peculiar nature of software development work, it has been suggested that such deputation of Technical Manpower abroad should not be considered detrimental to the benefits of the exemption under sections 10A, 10AA and 10B merely because such activities are rendered outside the eligible units/undertakings.

The matter has been examined. Explanation 3 to sections 10A and 10B and Explanation 2 to section 10AA clearly declare that profits and gains derived from "services for development of software" outside India would also be deemed as profits derived from export. It is therefore clarified that profits earned as a result of deployment of Technical Manpower at the client's place abroad specifically for software development work pursuant to a contract between the client and the eligible unit should not be denied benefits under sections 10A, 10AA and 10B provided such deputation of manpower is for the development of such software and all the prescribed conditions are fulfilled.

The extent to which the profits of the non-resident enterprise is to be attributed to the activities of such Permanent Establishment in India has been under consideration of the Board. 4. A non-resident or a foreign company is treated as having a Permanent Establishment in India under Article 5 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements entered into by India with different countries if the said non-resident or foreign company carries on business in India through a branch, sales office, etc., or through an agent (other than an independent agent) who habitually exercises an authority to conclude contracts or regularly delivers goods or merchandise or habitually secures orders on behalf of the non-resident principal. In such a case, the profits of the non-resident or foreign company attributable to the business activities carried out in India by the Permanent Establishment becomes taxable in India under Article 7 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement.

5. Paragraph 1 of Article 7 of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement provides that if a foreign enterprise carries on business in another country through a Permanent Establishment situated therein, the profits of the enterprise may be taxed in the other country but only so much of them as is attributable to the Permanent Establishment. Paragraph 2 of the same Article provides that subject to the provisions of Paragraph 3, there shall in each contracting State be attributed to that Permanent Establishment the profits which it might be expected to make if it were a distinct and separate enterprise engaged in the same or similar activities under the same or similar conditions and dealing wholly independently with the enterprise of which it is a Permanent Establishment. Paragraph 3 of the Article provides that in determining the profits of a Permanent Establishment there shall be allowed as deductions expenses which are incurred for the purposes of the Permanent Establishment including executive and general administrative expenses so incurred, whether in the State in which the Permanent Establishment is situated or elsewhere. What are the expenses that are deductible would have to be determined in accordance with the accepted principles of accountancy and the provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961.

6. Paragraph 2 contains the central directive on which the allocation of profits to a Permanent Establishment is intended to be based. The paragraph incorporates the view that the profits to be attributed to a Permanent Establishment are those which that Permanent Establishment would have made if instead of dealing with its Head Office, it had been dealing with an entirely separate enterprise under conditions and at prices prevailing in the ordinary market. This corresponds to the "arm's length principle". Paragraph 3 only provides a rule applicable for the determination of the profits of the Permanent Establishment, while paragraph 2 requires that the profits so determined correspond to the profit that a separate and independent enterprise would have made. Hence, in determining the profits attributable to an IT-enabled BPO unit constituting a Permanent Establishment, it will be necessary to determine the price of the services rendered by the Permanent Establishment to the Head Office or by the Head Office to the Permanent Establishment on the basis of "arm's length principle".

7. "Arm's length price" would have the same meaning as in the definition in section 92F(ii) of the Income-tax Act. The arm's length price would have to be determined in accordance with the provisions of sections 92 to 92F of the Act.
